## Column 1

->PREFACE<-

THE following facsimile of the New Testament text of the <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> <note>Latin for "The Sinai Book," a 4th-century Greek manuscript and one of the most important surviving witnesses to the biblical text</note> is made from negatives taken at St. Petersburg <note>then the capital of the Russian Empire, where the manuscript was held in the Imperial Library</note> by my wife and myself in the summer of 1908. In the library we were greatly helped by the courtesy of the officials, especially Dr. Bischoff and Dr. Papadopoulo Kerameus, who did everything possible to assist us, and outside we were so fortunate as to find in <note>original Dutch abbreviations: "Ds. and Mevr."</note> Reverend and Mrs. Pantekoek of the Dutch Church in St. Petersburg friends who were willing to take more trouble in forwarding our interests than many would have devoted to their own: the difficulty of finding an adequate dark room for the development of such large plates was considerable, and seemed likely to prove insuperable till our Dutch friends came to our rescue.

In the introductory pages I have had the benefit of consulting Dr. Kenyon and Sir George Warner in the British Museum and Dr. Hunt in Oxford, to the last of whom and to the authorities of the John Rylands Library, whose <term>Papyri</term> <note>ancient documents written on reed paper</note> he is editing, I owe the permission to reproduce a specimen of Rylands Papyr. 28. I am also greatly indebted to the Rev. Dr. Ehrle, S. J., Prefect of the Vatican Library, for his permission to print a specimen of the <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> <note>Another 4th-century Greek Bible, similar in age and importance to the Sinaiticus, housed in the Vatican</note>. My warmest thanks are due to my friend and former pupil Dr. J. de Zwaan, who spent much time and trouble in making lists of the various corrections in the <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>. These lists have, of course, a special value for the textual criticism of the New Testament, and I hope that Dr. de Zwaan and myself will be able in the course of time to publish some of the results which are based on them, in the direction of distinguishing the types of text which the various correctors preferred.

Finally, on behalf of my wife and myself, I must express a gratitude, in which I feel sure that those who may find the facsimile useful will join, to the Trustees of the Revision Surplus, Hort Memorial, and Hibbert Funds, and to the Governing Body of Magdalen College, for the grants of money which rendered possible our journey to St. Petersburg, as well as to the authorities of the Imperial Library for their permission to photograph their famous <term>Codex</term> <note>a manuscript in book form rather than a scroll</note>, and to the Delegates of the Oxford University Press for undertaking the publication.

->KIRSOPP LAKE.<-

LEIDEN, 1911.

->THE DISCOVERY OF THE CODEX<-

## Column 1

Tʜᴇ discovery of the <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term><note>The "Sinai Book," a 4th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible and one of the most important documents in biblical history.</note> by Tischendorf is one of the best-known stories in the history of <term>Palaeography</term><note>The study of ancient handwriting and the dating of historical manuscripts.</note>. In 1844 Tischendorf, who had planned a fresh critical edition of the New Testament, and had already visited most of the great libraries of the West, was travelling in the East in order to discover what new light might still be obtained from the monastic libraries. In the convent of St. Catherine on Mt. Sinai he found in a basket, which he understood to contain material for lighting the fire, forty-three leaves of the <term>Septuagint</term><note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>. These he obtained, and published in 1846 under the title of the *Codex of Frederick Augustus*¹<note>original: *Codex Frederico-Augustanus*</note>. This codex is now at Leipzig. He ascertained that the rest of the manuscript was in existence; and though he was unable to obtain possession of it, he cherished the hope of returning at some later period and of then being more successful. That in this way Tischendorf rightly earned the fame of discovering this valuable manuscript would be denied by no one; but M. Seymour de Ricci, in the *Archaeological Review*<note>original: *Revue Archéologique*</note>, 1909, p. 159, has recently pointed out that it was probably seen as early as 1761 by the Italian traveller, Vitaliano Donati, in his visit to Mt. Sinai. Donati's diary is still unpublished, but extracts were made from it by G. Lumbroso, in the *Proceedings of the Royal Lincean Academy*<note>original: *Atti della R. Accademia dei Lincei*</note> in 1879, in which on p. 501 the following statement is found: <note>original Italian: "In questo monastero ritrovai una quantità grandissima di codici membranacei . . . ve ne sono alcuni che mi sembravano anteriori al settimo secolo, ed in ispecie una Bibbia in membrane bellissime, assai grandi, sottili, e quadre, scritta in carattere rotondo e bellissimo; conservano poi in chiesa un Evangelistario greco in carattere d'oro rotondo, che dovrebbe pur essere assai antico."</note> ‘In this monastery I found a very great quantity of parchment codices . . . there are some which seemed to me earlier than the seventh century, and specifically a Bible on very beautiful parchment, quite large, thin, and square, written in a round and very beautiful script; they also keep in the church a Greek <term>Gospel Book</term><note>original: *Evangelistario*</note> in round gold script, which should also be quite ancient.’ The manuscript in gold letters is no doubt the *Golden Gospel Book*<note>original: *Evangelistarium Aureum*</note> (Gregory Lectionary 300) which is still shown to travellers, and the ‘Bible’ may well be, as

<column-break/>

## Column 2

M. de Ricci suggests, the Codex Sinaiticus. The objection that the script is described as ‘round’<note>original: *rotondo*</note> is adequately met by the fact that the *Golden Gospel Book*, which is also ‘round’, is an <term>uncial</term><note>A style of script written entirely in capital letters, common in ancient Greek and Latin manuscripts.</note>: no doubt Donati meant to distinguish the script from the narrow contracted type of uncial found in some late manuscripts.

After Tischendorf left the monastery, the manuscript seems to have been seen by two other scholars. In 1845 Porphyrius Uspenski¹ visited Sinai, and saw the manuscript—not only the remnant which Tischendorf had seen, but also the other parts to which it was now reunited. It would therefore seem that Tischendorf's conversation with the monks had aroused them to a sense of the value of their property. Porphyrius Uspenski also found some fragments of the manuscript in the bindings of other manuscripts.² Besides Porphyrius Uspenski it is generally thought that the manuscript was seen by Major Macdonald, a Scotsman who visited Sinai in 1848.³ Whether, however, this manuscript was really the Codex Sinaiticus or another manuscript of later date is doubted by Prof. Gregory⁴; fortunately the point is as unimportant as its discussion is indecisive.

In 1853 Tischendorf returned to Sinai, but could find no trace of the manuscript, or even discover whether it was still in the library. In 1859, however, he again visited the Mountain, armed with an introduction from the Tsar, and was warmly welcomed, but did not venture directly to approach the search for the manuscript until one evening he found a favourable opportunity for leading the conversation on to the subject of the

-> THE DISCOVERY OF THE CODEX <-

## Column 1

Septuagint. These tactics proved successful, and later on the steward <note>original: οἰκονόμος — the administrative official or bursar of a monastery</note>, desirous of showing that the monks also had a <term>MS.</term><note>Abbreviation for manuscript, a book written by hand.</note> of the <term>Septuagint</term><note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, brought him the Codex wrapped in a red cloth.<note>1</note> Tischendorf's delight can be imagined, when he found that it contained not only a great part of the Septuagint, but the whole of the New Testament, the Epistle of Barnabas, and part of the Shepherd of Hermas.

An arrangement was made with the monks that, if the superiors of the monastery, who were living at Cairo, were willing, the manuscript should be sent to Cairo to be copied. Hurriedly returning thither, Tischendorf persuaded the representatives of the monastery to make this concession, and, in consequence, a messenger was sent to St. Catherine's to fetch the manuscript, which on February 24, 1859, reached Cairo, where it was copied by Tischendorf and two assistants in the extraordinarily short space of two months. After this Tischendorf suggested to the monks at Cairo that the manuscript should be given to the Tsar.

There was, however, at that time an election in process to the archbishopric of Sinai;<note>2</note> a candidate had been unanimously selected, but he was not yet consecrated, and under these circumstances it was ultimately (in September 1859) agreed that Tischendorf should take the manuscript to the Tsar in anticipation of the formal gift which would be made when the archbishop was in a position to ratify it.

There has been much not very edifying controversy as to the terms on which this arrangement was made. Some of the monks have maintained that it was never their intention to make a permanent gift of the manuscript. Another version is that they bargained for a steamship to connect their harbour on the Red Sea with Port Said. Those who have had much to do with Oriental monks will understand how improbable it is that the terms of the arrangement, whatever it was, were ever known to any except a few of the leaders. The latter probably regarded the whole affair as a speculation. In any case, the fact is certain that Tischendorf was allowed by the archbishop to take the manuscript to St. Petersburg.

The Tsar was pleased to accept the present brought by Tischendorf; in November 1859, the manuscript was exhibited for a fortnight, and was then taken to Leipzig, in order that Tischendorf might issue a facsimile edition in accordance

## Column 2

with the Tsar's orders. Photography was not in those days sufficiently advanced to enable it to be employed, though Tischendorf considered its possibility, but special type was cut to imitate the manuscript, and the result may fairly claim to be the most perfect facsimile edition which was ever published in the pre-photographic period. It is a triumph of printing,<note>1</note> and Tischendorf's notes will always remain an indispensable aid to the study of the manuscript. It was issued in four volumes from St. Petersburg in 1862, under the title: THE SAINT PETERSBURG SINAI BOOK OF THE BIBLE. UNDER THE MOST AUGUST AUSPICES OF EMPEROR ALEXANDER II. BROUGHT FORTH FROM THE SHADOWS, TRANSPORTED TO EUROPE, AND EDITED TO ASSIST AND ILLUMINATE THE SACRED SCRIPTURES BY CONSTANTIN TISCHENDORF. <note>original Latin: BIBLIORUM CODEX SINAITICUS PETROPOLITANUS. AUSPICIIS AUGUSTISSIMIS IMPERATORIS ALEXANDRI II. EX TENEBRIS PROTRAXIT IN EUROPAM TRANSTULIT AD IUVANDAS ATQUE ILLUSTRANDAS SACRAS LITTERAS EDIDIT CONSTANTINUS TISCHENDORF.</note>

When the manuscript was no longer needed for the purposes of preparing this edition it was finally handed over to the Tsar, and deposited in the Imperial Library, where it is still to be seen in a special show case in the Great Hall.

Meanwhile the monks of Sinai had received nothing in return for their magnificent present;<note>2</note> and in a letter dated July 15, 1869, the Archbishop of Sinai hinted to Tischendorf that the time was approaching when the monks might reasonably expect some suitable acknowledgement. In consequence of this letter Tischendorf appears to have written to the Russian Ministry, and the result was that on November 18, 1869, 7,000 roubles were received by the monks of St. Catherine's, 2,000 roubles by the affiliated monastery of Mt. Thabor, and various decorations by the leading monks. The latter, however, have always claimed that they did not accept this as a satisfactory settlement, but no written protest on their part is known to exist, and the archbishop, at all events, remained on friendly terms with Tischendorf.<note>2</note>

Finally, it is perhaps sufficiently curious to deserve mention that Simonides the forger attempted to discredit the experts who had helped to detect his fraud, by claiming that he had himself written the Codex Sinaiticus, and had deceived them all; but the details of this absurd story belong rather to the annals of crime than to the history of <term>palaeography</term><note>The study of ancient handwriting.</note>.

<header>THE EARLIER HISTORY OF THE MS.</header>

## Column 1

->THE EARLIER HISTORY OF THE MS. ·<-

->THE CORRECTION OF THE CODEX AT<-
->CAESAREA<-

THE only point on which practical certainty can be
arrived at with regard to the history of the <term>MS.</term><note>Abbreviation for manuscript.</note> before it was
discovered by Tischendorf, is that at the time when one of the
correctors belonging to the group C was working it was in the
famous library at Caesarea. <note>An ancient city on the coast of Roman Palestine, a center of Christian scholarship.</note> Palaeographical <note>The study of ancient handwriting.</note> and historical
grounds agree to fix this time as not later than the beginning
of the seventh or earlier than that of the fifth century.
   The library at Caesarea is one of the three great Christian
libraries¹ known to have existed in the third century. It is
perhaps correct to speak of Pamphilus <note>A scholar and martyr (d. 309 AD) who was the teacher of the historian Eusebius.</note> as the founder of this
library,² but the nucleus of his collection was the MSS. of
Origen, <note>One of the most influential early Christian theologians and scholars.</note> who in turn probably inherited the library of Juliana
which is mentioned by Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History vi. 17*), who says,
"Origen indicates that he received these, along with other interpretations of the Scriptures by Symmachus, from a certain Juliana, who he says had inherited the books from Symmachus himself." <note>original: Ταῦτα δὲ ὁ Ὠριγένης μετὰ καὶ ἄλλων εἰς τὰς γραφὰς ἑρμηνειῶν τοῦ Συμμάχου σημαίνει παρὰ Ἰουλιανῆς τινος εἰληφέναι, ἣν καί φησι παρ’ αὐτοῦ Συμμάχου τὰς βίβλους διαδέξασθαι.</note> The actual words
of Origen’s statement are given by Palladius (*Lausiac History lxiv*,
ed. Butler), who says, "I found these things written in a very old stichometric <note>A book written in lines of specific length to measure the size of the text.</note> book, written by the hand of Origen: 'I found this book at the house of Juliana the virgin in Caesarea, when I was hiding at her place; she said she had received it from Symmachus himself, the translator of the Jews.'" <note>original: εὗρον δὲ ταῦτα ἐγὼ γεγραμμένα ἐν τῷ παλαιοτάτῳ βιβλίῳ στιχηρῷ, ἐγέγραπτο χειρὶ Ὠριγένους· Τοῦτο τὸ βιβλίον εὗρον ἐγὼ παρὰ Ἰουλιανῇ τῇ παρθένῳ ἐν Καισαρείᾳ, κρυπτόμενος παρ’ αὐτῇ, ἥτις ἔλεγε παρ’ αὐτοῦ Συμμάχου τοῦ ἑρμηνέως τῶν Ἰουδαίων αὐτὸ εἰληφέναι.</note> Unfortunately the copy-
ist of this note was apparently not very accurate, and thought
that Caesarea in Cappadocia was indicated, but it is probable
that this is merely a mistake and that Caesarea in Palestine
was really intended. In any case there is little reason to

   According to Jerome (*On Illustrious Men 3. 113*) the library began
to show signs of decay at the end of the fourth century, and

This statement may

Caesarea was used by Paul of Tella for the Syriac Hexapla,
as is stated in the subscriptions to the various books of the Old
Testament;⁴ but after this there is no proof of the continued
existence of the library. Its fate is unknown; but Caesarea
was taken by the Arabs in 638, and we may guess with much
probability that the library was dispersed or destroyed.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly introduction to the history of the Codex Sinaiticus. It focuses on the physical evidence—specifically "colophons" or end-notes—that link this manuscript to the famous library of Caesarea and the work of early Christian martyrs Pamphilus and Antoninus.</meta>

<page-num>viii</page-num>
<header>THE EARLIER HISTORY OF THE MS.</header>

## Column 1

Friderico-Augustanus <note>Latin: "The Frederick-Augustus [Codex]," the name given to the portion of the manuscript held in Leipzig.</note>). It has often been stated that these
notes are by the corrector C, but this is not the case, as will
be seen when the facsimile of the Old Testament is published.
There is a certain family resemblance between C and the scribe
of the notes at the end of Ezra and Esther, but they are not
identical, and there is perhaps a difference of ink—C used
a redder, and the scribe of the note at the end of Esther a
yellower colour—though I am inclined to doubt this, strikingly
evident though it seems at first. The two notes happen to
have been written on bad patches of vellum <note>High-quality parchment made from animal skin.</note>, which have not
taken the ink well, so that the writing has faded, but at the
end of the note to Ezra, where the parchment improves, the
ink has the same reddish tint as C. Further discussion of
this point belongs to the introduction to the Old Testament:
it is sufficient here to say that the probable solution of the
question is that several scribes (of which C was certainly one)
were engaged in correcting the text according to that of the
Codex Pamphili <note>The "Book of Pamphilus," a lost but famous master-copy of the Bible.</note>, and one of them (not C) wrote the notes at
the end of Esther and Ezra to explain what had been done.
That the writer of the notes belongs to the C group of scribes
is tolerably certain, and his statements make it almost equally
plain that this group was formed by the monks in the scrip-
torium <note>A room in a monastery dedicated to the copying of manuscripts.</note> at Caesarea. The text of the notes is as follows:—

(1) *At the end of Ezra* (Cod. Frid.-Aug. f. 13).

->It was collated against a very<-
->ancient copy<-
->corrected by the hand of the<-
->holy martyr Pamphilus,<-
->which copy had at the<-
->end a certain subscription<-
->in his own hand situated below,<-
->reading as follows:<-
->"It was transcribed and corrected<-
->according to the Hexapla of Origen <note>A massive six-columned comparative edition of the Old Testament compiled by the scholar Origen in the 3rd century.</note>;<-

-> THE EARLIER HISTORY OF THE MANUSCRIPT. <-

## Column 1

Caesarea is not absolutely demonstrative; it is possible that the manuscript of Pamphilus <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD) was a scholar and martyr who assembled a famous library of biblical texts.</note> had been taken to some other place, and of course the view that all the **C** correctors belong to much the same place and time is a point on which it is possible that other opinions will be held when the facsimile <note>An exact photographic reproduction.</note> of the Old Testament completes the presentation of the evidence. It is therefore all the more satisfactory that there is some indirect evidence for connecting another of the **C** group — **C<sup>a</sup>** — with the use of a manuscript of Pamphilus in the Pauline epistles.

It will be noted that the colophons <note>A colophon is a finishing stroke or note at the end of a manuscript providing details about its production.</note> at the ends of Ezra and Esther only refer to manuscripts of a comparatively small part of the Old Testament, and there are no other notes elsewhere. It is, however, well known that in the Pauline epistles critics¹ have long been struck by the resemblance between the text of the corrector **C<sup>a</sup>** and that of the codex **H<sup>paul</sup>**. Now, codex **H<sup>paul</sup>** has at the end of the Pauline epistles a long colophon, beginning with the name Evagrios², and ending with the statement: —

-> This book was compared <note>original Greek: Ἀντεβλήθη δὲ ἡ βίβλος</note> <-
-> against the copy in Caesarea <note>original: πρὸς τὸ ἐν Καισαρίᾳ ἀντίγραφον</note> <-
-> from the library <-
-> of Saint Pamphilus, <-
-> written by his [own] hand³ <note>original: τῆς βιβλιοθήκης τοῦ ἁγίου Παμφίλου χειρὶ γεγραμμένον [αὐτοῦ]</note> <-

Considering the close textual relationship between codex **H<sup>paul</sup>** and the corrector **C<sup>a</sup>** of the Codex Sinaiticus, it is legitimate to regard this evidence as increasing the probability that during the time that the corrector **C<sup>a</sup>** was working the Codex Sinaiticus was in the library at Caesarea, in which there were certainly many manuscripts of Pamphilus, rather than in some other library to which a manuscript of Pamphilus might have been brought.

The date which must be assigned to the time when the Codex was in Caesarea depends entirely on that which palaeography <note>The study of ancient handwriting to determine the age and origin of documents.</note> gives to the writing of the **C** correctors, and especially of course to that of the scribe who wrote the notes at the end of Ezra and Esther. On this point opinions are likely

<column-break/>

## Column 2

to differ. The latest date suggested is the seventh century; the earliest is the fifth. Dr. F. G. Kenyon and Dr. A. S. Hunt agree in regarding the sixth century as possible, but the former is inclined to accept the seventh as equally possible, while the latter is more disposed to prefer an earlier date.

-> THE HISTORY OF THE MANUSCRIPT AFTER <-
-> IT WAS IN CAESAREA <-

How or when the manuscript passed from Caesarea to Sinai is absolutely unknown. There is not a trace of evidence. The monastery of St. Catherine’s on Mt. Sinai was one of the foundations of Justinian, and from the sixth century it became one of the strongholds of the Greek Church and the Malkite Syrians <note>Members of the Christian community in the Levant who remained loyal to the Byzantine Emperor and the Council of Chalcedon.</note>. Caesarea, on the other hand, was taken by the Arabs in 638. It is therefore a plausible guess that the manuscript was taken to Sinai by refugees from Caesarea. But this is merely a guess: it may have been taken to many places after leaving Caesarea and have reached Sinai many years or centuries later.

-> THE ORIGINAL PROVENANCE AND <-
-> DATE OF THE MANUSCRIPT <-

The only points in the pre-Caesarean history of the manuscript which repay discussion are concerned with the place and time of its original writing, for from the day that it passed out of the scriptorium <note>The room in a monastery or library where manuscripts were copied.</note> until the time that it was revised at Caesarea there is no other evidence of any kind to throw light on its history. It is of course true that the correctors **Bᵃ**, **B**, and possibly **A³**, **A⁴**, and **A⁵**, may have done their work outside the scriptorium, but there is nothing in their scripts to justify any suggestion that they belonged to one locality rather than another, and they are (see p. xxiii), if not contemporary with the original scribes, at least extremely close to them in age.

The *terminus a quo* <note>Latin: "The limit from which," meaning the earliest possible date.</note>, from which the date of the manuscript must be reckoned, is provided by the fact that the Eusebian apparatus <note>A system of cross-referencing the four Gospels, developed by Eusebius of Caesarea in the early 4th century.</note> was added to it before it was issued from the scriptorium (see p. xix). It is unfortunate that we do not know the exact date when Eusebius made his apparatus, but it is

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins and dating of the Codex Sinaiticus. While the previous page discussed the manuscript's connection to the library at Caesarea through its correctors, this section evaluates the physical evidence of the handwriting to determine if it was originally created in Egypt or Palestine during the 4th century.</meta>

-> THE ORIGINAL PROVENANCE AND DATE OF THE MS. <-

## Column 1

It is at least plain that the first quarter of the fourth century is the earliest date which has any reasonable probability. The latest possible date <note>original Latin: *terminus ad quem*</note> cannot be so easily fixed. We are here entirely dependent on the study of ancient handwriting <note>original: palaeographical considerations</note>, and on the comparison of the writing with that of papyri. The earliest vellum <term>vellum</term> <note>High-quality animal skin used as a writing surface before paper became common.</note> manuscript of which the date can approximately be fixed is the Vienna Codex of Dioscorides, which cannot be far removed from the year 500. No one doubts but that the Codex Sinaiticus and various other manuscripts are earlier than this; but the history of writing shows that the development of handwritings is by no means regular, and decisive dating is usually very difficult. 

Nevertheless, a comparison with papyri suggests that the Codex Sinaiticus is more likely to belong to the fourth than to the fifth century; Dr. Hunt, indeed, expressed the view that if it had not been for the evidence of the Eusebian cross-references <note>original: Eusebian apparatus; a system created by Eusebius of Caesarea to help readers find parallel passages in the four Gospels.</note>, he should have not regarded the third century as an impossible date. This view of the date of the manuscript is based on the assumption that the origin <note>original: provenance</note> of the manuscript is the same as that of the papyri—Egyptian; but an element of doubt cannot be excluded on this point, and it is clear that if the assumption be baseless, the date is proportionately less certain. 

Baseless, however, the assumption fortunately is not: as will be shown, an Egyptian origin is actually the most probable for the Codex Sinaiticus; but it is not certain, and there have been competent scholars who have been inclined to think that Caesarea <note>An ancient city on the coast of Roman Palestine, famous for its Christian library.</note> not only was the resting-place of the manuscript in the sixth century, but also has the best claim to be regarded as its original home. Of the various arguments, partly historical and partly handwriting-based, bearing on this point, those which are purely based on handwriting are likely to seem rather unsatisfactory to those who are acquainted with the splendid results reached by Latin scholars in fixing the date and origin of their manuscripts. It is, however, the fact, regrettable though it be, that this line of research is much less fruitful in Greek than in Latin documents. We have not sufficient specimens of ascertained date and diverse origin to justify any security of judgement. The formal literary handwriting style <note>original: literary hand</note> in papyri, which affords our only guide in this matter, is an excessively fixed type, which those who are constantly engaged in papyrus research are least prepared to date with exactness, and as the papyri all come from the same country, they afford little or no evidence 
<margin>x</margin>

<column-break/>

## Column 2

as to local peculiarities of script. It is indeed now possible to state with a certainty which was hitherto unattainable that this or that type of letter was common in Egyptian papyri, but it is not possible to say that it was characteristic, in the sense that it was absent in other schools of beautiful writing <note>original: calligraphy</note>; for we are almost ignorant of the history of literary hands as distinct from private hands outside of Egypt. 

Moreover, we do not know with any precision what changes may have been introduced by professional scribes when they passed from writing on papyrus to the somewhat different surface of vellum. The only analogy which we can study—that of the revival of small-letter script <note>original: minuscule revival</note> in the ninth century—is imperfect in kind and remote in date. In that century, professional scribes on vellum began to abandon the large capital letters <note>original: uncial character</note>, which they had taken over from the formal handwriting of the papyri, in favour of a cursive <note>A flowing, "joined-up" style of handwriting.</note> hand modelled on the earlier private hands. Obviously it is impossible to argue from this great revolution to the small one of passing from papyrus to vellum; but it is perhaps admissible to point out that as the changes made in the ninth century from the private cursive hand were comparatively small, all the more so <note>original Latin: *à fortiori*</note> those in the fourth were probably smaller. 

With these serious qualifications, comparison with papyri affords the only handwriting-based clue to the origin of the Codex Sinaiticus. It tends to suggest that the papyri and the Codex come from the same place. There are no letters in the Codex Sinaiticus which cannot be paralleled in papyri of the fourth or earlier centuries. The three forms which attract attention in the Codex Sinaiticus are the so-called Coptic Mu <note>The letter 'M' written in a style that became standard in the Egyptian Coptic script.</note>, the curious shaped Omega <note>The Greek letter for a long 'O'.</note> with a long central line, and an occasional use of the cursive Xi <note>The Greek letter for 'X'.</note>. The Coptic Mu is common in papyri: it is called Coptic because it happens to be the form which passed over into the Coptic alphabet; but there is no evidence to show that it was rare outside of Egypt. 

The long Omega is much more rare: it is found in Rylands Papyrus 28, a papyrus of probably the fourth century, but Dr. Hunt was not able to quote any other instance of its use in papyri, nor is it common in vellum manuscripts. I only know of it in the Codex Vaticanus, and here too it is comparatively rare. The use of the cursive Xi in large-letter <note>original: uncial</note> script is also rare: it is found in the additions of the corrector **A<sup>2</sup>** in the Codex Sinaiticus, in the titles and sections of Codex Vaticanus, in Rylands Papyrus 28, and in Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 852. (2) The word **"Israelite"** <note>original: Ἰσραηλείτης (Israeleites)</note> occurs nine times in the New Testament; and in eight of them the Codex Sinaiticus spells it with an extra "t" sound as **Istraeleites** <note>original: Ἰστραηλείτης</note>. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins of the Codex Sinaiticus, focusing on whether it shares a common origin with the Codex Vaticanus. It evaluates handwriting evidence (palaeography) and specific spelling habits (orthography) to link the two manuscripts to the same professional writing room, likely in Egypt or Caesarea.</meta>

as early as any which can be cited in Latin, and even if it is ultimately a Latin-style expression, it provides no argument against the Egyptian origin of any individual manuscript.

Thus, the argument from spelling does nothing to challenge the likelihood of the Egyptian origin of the Codex Sinaiticus, and in the case of the word <term>krabaktos</term> <note>original Greek: κράβακτος; a term for a "bed" or "pallet" often found in Egyptian Greek.</note>, it even provides somewhat strong support. However, it is important to remember that spelling and <term>palaeography</term> <note>The study of ancient handwriting styles.</note> can only identify the nationality of the scribe, not the physical location of the <term>scriptorium</term> <note>A professional writing room or workshop for producing books.</note>: there is always a probability that an Egyptian was writing in Egypt, but he may have been living in a foreign land.

A further argument, which is partly but not mainly based on handwriting, seeks to link the Codex Sinaiticus with the Codex Vaticanus <note>The other major 4th-century Greek Bible, kept in the Vatican Library.</note>, and thus establish that they were made in the same place. This argument is somewhat complicated and is best divided into three stages. First, there is the question of the physical relationship between the handwriting of the two volumes; the most famous point here is the attempt made by Tischendorf <note>Constantine von Tischendorf, the 19th-century scholar who discovered the Codex Sinaiticus.</note> to identify the scribe of the Codex Vaticanus as the same person who served as "Scribe D" (who is also the "Corrector A²") of the Codex Sinaiticus. Secondly, there is the study by Dr. Rahlfs connecting the Codex Vaticanus with Athanasius <note>A prominent 4th-century Bishop of Alexandria.</note>; and thirdly, there is an attempt first made by Dr. Rendel Harris, and later more fully by Dr. Armitage Robinson, to connect both manuscripts with "Euthalius" and probably with the city of Caesarea <note>A major center of Christian learning in Palestine.</note>.

Tischendorf’s view that the main body of the text of the Codex Vaticanus was written by Scribe D of the Codex Sinaiticus is, unfortunately, impossible to defend.¹ A comparison of the two handwriting styles, which can easily be made on Plate III, will convince anyone of this fact. It would be absurd to argue that on that plate, the hand that wrote column 3 is different from the hand that wrote column 2, yet identical to the hand that wrote column 4; and yet, this is the very claim that Tischendorf’s theory requires. If one argues that there is an even greater difference between column 3 (the work of Scribe D) and the handwriting of Corrector A², which are nevertheless considered to be by the same hand, the answer is that these cases are not of the same type. Corrector A² and Scribe D may be the same person

---

¹ This is, I may add, the opinion of every handwriting expert who has seen the proofs of this reproduction. I have found none who are inclined to agree with Tischendorf, or even to hesitate on the matter.

## Column 2

despite a superficially great difference in script, because two different styles of writing were used for the main text and for the corrections. The same scribe may write many distinct styles of handwriting, but the point is that he will not write the same *style* in two different ways. The script of Corrector A² is distinct in style from that of Scribe D, while the script of the Codex Vaticanus is the same style as Scribe D’s, but written in a different manner. It is therefore necessary to abandon Tischendorf’s view that part of the text of the Codex Vaticanus was written by the same scribe who wrote the text of the Codex Sinaiticus. 

Nevertheless, if the main text is set aside, there is a high probability that the two manuscripts came from the same professional workshop. This view is based on the remarkable similarity between the hands of the scribes who added the titles to the book of Acts in both manuscripts. Typical examples of these are placed together in the fourth column of Plate III, and it will be seen that the resemblance is so great that it is impossible to say with complete confidence that they are not by the same person. Especially noticeable is the appearance of the cursive <term>xi</term> <note>The Greek letter 'x', written here in a more flowing, joined-up style (ξ).</note> in the middle of an otherwise <term>uncial</term> <note>A formal style of writing using large, rounded capital letters.</note> script. I am, however, convinced that it is more likely that we are dealing with two different hands from the same workshop. The tail of the <term>xi</term> is more carefully rounded in the Codex Vaticanus, and the <term>iota</term> <note>The Greek letter 'i' (ι).</note> in the second syllable of the word <term>Praxeis</term> <note>original Greek: πράξεις; the Greek title for the Book of "Acts".</note> is exaggeratedly long in the Codex Sinaiticus; these differences, which are consistent, seem sufficient to distinguish the two writers. 

Nevertheless, the similarity is extremely great and is hardly explainable unless we assume that both writers were trained in the same workshop. Alternatively, the differences might simply mean that there is a gap in time between the two examples—that is to say, the word <term>Acts</term> in the Codex Vaticanus was written by a scribe in his youth, and the <term>Acts</term> in the Codex Sinaiticus was written by that same person in his old age. But whether this is true or not is not of great importance: the significant point is that there is, in any case, good evidence for thinking that these two great Bibles come from the same workshop, despite the fact that Tischendorf was wrong in thinking they were written by the exact same person. The only possibilities that could weaken this evidence are: (1) it may be that the significant titles for <term>Acts</term> were written by two scribes who learned in the same school but worked in different workshops; or (2) it may be that the

## Column 1

headings <note>The text refers to "superscriptions," which are the titles or labels written at the top of pages.</note> in the Codex Vaticanus¹ were added after it had passed outside the original <term>scriptorium</term> <note>A professional workshop where manuscripts were copied.</note> to some other place. These are real possibilities, and regarding the latter, attention may be directed to Dr. Karl Dziatzko’s *Investigations into Selected Chapters of Ancient Book-making* <note>original German: "Untersuchungen über ausgewählte Kapitel des antiken Buchwesens"</note>, especially to his seventh chapter, 'The Influence of the Scroll-form on the Codex-form.' In this, he adopts the view that the custom of adding page-headings did not exist before the end of the fourth century, and points out that the Codex Vaticanus represents a transitional period, in which the addition was not made by the original scribe. His theory seems to be supported by the evidence of the headings in the Codex Sinaiticus (see p. xxi).

It will, however, probably not be denied that there is, despite all other possibilities, a probability that the Codex Sinaiticus and the Codex Vaticanus belonged to the same scriptorium. Where, then, ought we to look for it? It was suggested above that the fact that the Egyptian Papyrus Rylands 28 agrees with the two codices in practically the only <term>palaeographical</term> <note>The study of ancient handwriting and its development over time.</note> peculiarities which they present must be regarded as pointing to Egypt until contradictory evidence be discovered. So far, however, from refuting this suggestion, Dr. Rahlfs—who investigated the historical and critical evidence for the origin and date of the Codex Vaticanus in the *Reports of the Royal Society of Sciences in Göttingen*² <note>original German: "Nachrichten der königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen"</note>—has strongly supported it.

He has pointed out that the Codex Vaticanus agrees in the most remarkable way with the list of scriptural books given by Athanasius <note>A powerful Bishop of Alexandria in the 4th century.</note> in his Paschal letter for the year 367. The points of agreement against other authorities are these: (1) In the Old Testament, the book of Esther is not reckoned among the books which are canonical <note>original Greek: κανονιζόμενα; books officially recognized as part of the Bible.</note>, but only among those which are for public reading <note>original Greek: ἀναγιγνωσκόμενα; books considered useful for teaching but not equal to the core scriptures.</note>. (2) In the New Testament, in Codex Vaticanus, the book of Hebrews is placed between the "Epistles of the Captivity" <note>Letters traditionally thought to be written by St. Paul while in prison, such as Ephesians and Philippians.</note> and the Pastoral Epistles. This agrees with the Greek and Syriac text of the Paschal letter; but the <term>Sahidic version</term> <note>A translation of the Bible into the dialect of Southern Egypt.</note>, agreeing with the usual Sahidic biblical text, places it between Corinthians and Galatians. It is argued that this represents

<column-break/>

## Column 2

in a Sahidic text a return to an old local use in Egypt; and, curiously enough, Codex Vaticanus has a continuous numbering for the sections in the epistles, which is at present dislocated in such a way as to show that it was taken from a manuscript which placed Hebrews after Galatians. This is not quite the same as the Sahidic, but Dr. Rahlfs thinks that it is near enough to justify the view that the Codex Vaticanus is an attempt to carry out Athanasius's views as to the order of the books, and that the text of the <term>archetype</term> <note>The original or older manuscript from which the current one was copied.</note>, which was being modified, belonged to the old Egyptian type represented by the Sahidic Version. He therefore argues that the Codex Vaticanus comes from Alexandria and is at least as late as 367.

It is of course plain that this is not a decisive argument: the parallel between the Sahidic text of Athanasius and that implied by the numbering in Codex Vaticanus is not quite perfect; and the textual facts in connection with Athanasius are by no means clear. Nevertheless, when all these points have been discounted, it will probably be agreed that there remains enough to justify the statement that, as our knowledge stands at present, there is a presumption in favor of Egypt as the original home of the Codex Vaticanus. One may also, without unduly venturing into the field of textual criticism, here draw attention to a further point. The Psalms quoted in the Coptic text of the *Pistis Sophia* <note>A 3rd or 4th-century Gnostic text discovered in Egypt.</note> have an extraordinary resemblance to the text of the Codex Sinaiticus—in Prof. Harnack's phrase,¹ "This text stands as close to the Codex Sinaiticus as a twin brother" <note>original German: "Dieser Text steht dem Cod. Sinait. wie ein Zwillingsbruder nahe."</note>. This fact may be allowed to weigh the scales in favor of an Egyptian origin. Formerly, one would have regarded Egypt as, in this connection, synonymous with Alexandria; but in view of the wealth of Greek papyri from Oxyrhynchus and other places remote from Alexandria, it is necessary to hesitate, though it probably remains true that splendid volumes, such as the Codex Sinaiticus and the Codex Vaticanus, are more likely to have been produced in Alexandria than in the country higher up the Nile.

It remains to consider the connection between the two codices and "Euthalius" <note>An ancient editor of the New Testament whose work influenced the way the letters of the apostles were divided into chapters and verses.</note>. The simplest way of dealing with this point is to begin by summarizing the points connected

    There are found in many Greek manuscripts <note>original: MSS.</note> and in many versions the traces of something resembling a critical edition of the Acts and Epistles, giving a series of prologues and chapter divisions, and dividing the text <term>stichometrically</term> <note>Written in lines of varying length to match the sense or rhythm of the sentence, rather than in fixed column widths.</note>. Traditionally this edition was made by Euthalius—an unknown person who is sometimes referred to as a deacon, sometimes as a bishop, sometimes of Alexandria, sometimes of Soulka, which is probably Sulci in Sardinia. It is, however, one of the many difficulties connected with this question that critics are not agreed as to whether the name of Euthalius, or at least the name of Sulci, be not a later growth in the tradition.
It is therefore wiser at present to speak of ‘Euthalius’ rather than Euthalius, in order to show that the name is used as a symbol for the original author of this edition of Acts and Epistles, rather than as the name of an historical person. At one point in its history this edition was compared with the manuscripts of Pamphilus in Caesarea <note>Pamphilus was a 3rd-century scholar who founded a famous Christian library in Caesarea.</note> by a certain Evagrius whose name is found in the <term>colophon</term> <note>A finishing note at the end of a manuscript providing details about its production.</note> attached to Codex H of the Letters of Paul <note>original: Cod. H$^{\text{paul}}$</note>—the oldest manuscript of the ‘Euthalian’ edition. In this respect the history of the edition is precisely similar to that of the Codex Sinaiticus, which was corrected by a "C" corrector by means of the same manuscripts in parts of the Old Testament; but this does not prove that the edition was originally made in Caesarea, any more than it proves that the Codex Sinaiticus was written there. Now, among the characteristics of the earliest form of this edition—belonging, that is to say, to the original ‘Euthalian’ <term>recension</term> <note>A specific version of a text that has been revised or edited.</note>, and not due to the further work of Evagrius—is a rather elaborate system of dividing the Acts into chapters, and these chapters into smaller divisions, and a corrupt form of the same system is found both in the Codex Sinaiticus and the Codex Vaticanus. That this is so is the discovery of Dr. Armitage Robinson,$^{1}$ who has shown that though both <term>codices</term> <note>The plural of codex; early books made of bound leaves rather than scrolls.</note> have the same corrupt form, each has mistakes which the other has avoided. In the Codex Sinaiticus the chapter divisions were added by the corrector A$^{2}$, who worked in the <term>scriptorium</term> <note>The room in a monastery or library where manuscripts were copied.</note>, and it is usually stated that in Codex Vaticanus they were also added by a very early hand. From this therefore Dr. Armitage Robinson concluded that the numeration ‘must go back to a common source—some manuscript which gave its numeration to them both: and this seems

In the second place it is important because the only clue—admittedly a slight one—which we possess for the provenance of ‘Euthalius’ is that in the prologue to Acts the whole is dedicated to Athanasius <note>A powerful Bishop of Alexandria in the 4th century.</note>. It is true that critics have doubted the authenticity and the meaning of this dedication; but they have done so partly on erroneous theories as to the date of ‘Euthalius’. There is not in fact any reason why he should not have been a younger contemporary of the great Athanasius. In any case, so far as it goes, this tradition certainly lends support to the theory that the Codex Sinaiticus came from an Egyptian provenance.
    All these arguments point to Egypt, but inasmuch as they are not quite conclusive, it is necessary to point out the one serious argument which really seems to direct us to Caesarea for the provenance of the Codex Sinaiticus. It possesses the <term>Eusebian canons</term> <note>A system of ten tables used to help readers find and compare parallel passages across the four Gospels, created by Eusebius of Caesarea.</note>, and the earlier the date assigned to the manuscript, the more probable, it may be thought, is it that a manuscript containing these canons should come from Caesarea. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nevertheless the obvious force of this argument must be discounted by the fact that in considering the probability of one locality over another with reference to the early use of the Eusebian apparatus, the important point is really not the place in which Eusebius wrote, but the place in which Carpianus, to whom it was sent, received it. Now, our ignorance as to Carpianus is complete. He may have been a Caesarean, or he may have been an Alexandrian, or Byzantine: we know nothing about him, and therefore when we are discussing the provenance of the <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> <note>One of the world's oldest and most important Bibles, dating to the mid-4th century.</note> we have really not much more right to use the Eusebian canons as an argument in favour of Caesarea than we have to use the <term>Ammonian sections</term> <note>An older system of dividing the Gospels into numbered sections, traditionally attributed to a scholar from Alexandria.</note>, which are traditionally ascribed to an Alexandrian scholar, as evidence for an Egyptian origin. It must also be noted that the Caesarean theory has gained additional attractiveness from the hypothesis so often put forward, that the Codex Sinaiticus is one of the manuscripts <note>original: MSS.</note> which Constantine instructed Eusebius to have made for Constantinople.¹ But it should be observed that this theory is not confirmed by the fact that the manuscript <note>original: MS.</note> was in the library at Caesarea—not in Constantinople—in the sixth century.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;There is also a further point which may be regarded as counting against Caesarea. In the note attached to Matthew 2:15 a scribe contemporary with the manuscript, and working on it before it actually issued from the <term>scriptorium</term> <note>A dedicated room for copying manuscripts, usually in a monastery or library.</note>, has given Numbers <note>original: ἐν ἀριθμοῖς</note> as the source of the quotation "Out of Egypt I called my son" <note>original: ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐκάλεσα τὸν υἱόν μου</note>. Moreover, the suggestion is clearly untenable if Rahlfs’s view be accepted as to the date as well as the provenance of the Codex Vaticanus, which, as we have seen, ought probably to be regarded as belonging to the same place and time as the Codex Sinaiticus, for according to his view the Codex Vaticanus is not earlier than 367. Personally, however, I do not regard his theory to be as cogent with regard to the date as it is to the provenance of the manuscript.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Even, however, if this connexion between Athanasius and the Codex Sinaiticus be given up as a guess which is too uncertain to render its consideration desirable, it remains true that all the arguments from history, criticism, <term>palaeography</term> <note>The study of ancient handwriting to date and identify manuscripts.</note>, and <term>orthography</term> <note>Spelling conventions.</note> combine to give to the view that the codex is an Egyptian manuscript of the fourth century a probability which cannot be approached by any other theory. It would be too much to call it certain: but short of this it may fairly be regarded as the hypothesis which ought to be used as the general basis of any discussions as to the critical value of the Codex Sinaiticus.

<meta>This page transitions from the historical discussion of the manuscript’s origins (the debates between Caesarea and Alexandria) to a physical, technical description of the object itself. It moves from "where was it made?" to "what is it made of?"</meta>

## Column 1

->DESCRIPTION OF THE CODEX<-

The technical description of a manuscript ought logically to begin with the binding—the first thing to catch the eye of the observer—and thence to work through the various questions concerned with the vellum, the ‘make-up’ of the leaves, and the ink, to the more complicated problems of the differentiation of scribes and correctors. The <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> <note>One of the oldest and most important surviving hand-written copies of the Bible, dating to the 4th century.</note>, however, had lost its binding before <term>Tischendorf</term> <note>Constantin von Tischendorf, the 19th-century German biblical scholar who recovered the manuscript from St. Catherine's Monastery.</note> discovered it, and therefore the only points to be discussed are those concerned with the vellum and ink, and the differentiation of the scribes and correctors.

->THE VELLUM AND INK<-

The manuscript is written on fine <term>parchment</term> <note>Also called vellum; a writing surface made from specially treated animal skins.</note> made from the skin of some rather large animal—Tischendorf suggested an antelope, but in view of the manner in which this guess has been copied by successive writers on the text of the New Testament, and the certainty with which much repetition seems to have invested it in their eyes, it is perhaps not unnecessary to point out that there is nothing in the vellum to indicate an antelope rather than any other animal of the requisite size. It varies considerably in thickness: and the thicker leaves, which have generally preserved the writing better than the thin ones, are inclined to a yellowish tint. Many of the leaves are so thin that the writing from the other side is sometimes so plainly visible as to become confusing, and in a few cases the ink has eaten through the vellum so as to leave holes. As a rule, however, the vellum struck me as not quite so thin as that of the <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> <note>Another 5th-century Greek Bible, one of the three great "uncial" (capital letter) codices.</note>, and to have consequently suffered somewhat less from erosion.

The edges of the leaves have been slightly trimmed since the time of the **C correctors** <note>A group of editors who revised the manuscript, likely in the 7th century.</note>; this can be seen, for instance, on folio 49 <term>recto</term> <note>The front side of a leaf, or the right-hand page.</note>. So far as it is now possible to discover, there is no writing on the edges of the closed manuscript.

->xvi<-

<column-break/>

## Column 2

The Codex was prepared for writing in the usual way by rulings to regulate the lines and columns. There are, apparently always, 48 lines, and each of the four columns is regulated by a vertical line on each side. The <term>prickings</term> <note>Small holes made with a sharp tool at the edge of the sheet to guide the drawing of straight lines.</note> which were always made at the edge of the leaves as a guide for the preparer of the vellum have been cut away, but in a few places a mistake seems to have been made by the preparer of the vellum, and a line of prickings can still be seen in the middle of the first column of writing.

The <term>gatherings</term> <note>Also called quires; sections of the book formed by folding sheets of parchment together before binding.</note> into which the sheets of vellum were made up are as a rule <term>quaternions</term> <note>A gathering of four sheets of parchment folded once to create eight leaves (sixteen pages).</note> of four <term>conjugate leaves</term> <note>Leaves that form a single continuous piece of parchment.</note>, but 78 <note>original: "$\overline{οη}$"</note> (in Luke) has only seven <term>folia</term> <note>Individual leaves or pages.</note>, 80 <note>original: "$\overline{π}$"</note> (the end of the Gospels) and 6 <note>original: "$\overline{ς}$"</note> (in Barnabas) have six each, and 101 <note>original: "$\overline{ρα}$"</note> (the end of Barnabas) has only two. <note>¹ These numbers are those of the recent signatures.</note> <note>² Nothing is missing from this gathering: therefore the suggestion that the Codex contained something between Barnabas and Hermas falls to the ground.</note> Each gathering appears to have been <term>signed</term> <note>Marked with a "signature," a number used by the binder to keep the sections in the right order.</note> in a dull red ink at the top left-hand corner of the first recto by a hand which was probably contemporary with the manuscript. It is therefore likely that these signatures ought to be reckoned among the work of the scribes who were employed in the original <term>scriptorium</term> <note>A room in a monastery or library where manuscripts were copied.</note>, though there is no proof that this was the case. Most of these signatures have been cut off, but traces of them can be seen in the Epistles and later books. The best specimen will be found on folio 86$^{r}$. A later scribe, perhaps as recent as the eighth century (it is impossible to fix the period of isolated figures with even approximate certainty), has added fresh signatures in the right-hand top corner of the first recto of each gathering. It will, however, be noted that his numbers are less by a single unit than those of the original numerator, and in the older signatures the right-hand figure has consistently been erased; it can, however, still be read on folio 78$^{r}$. Either the original numerator made a mistake—a supposition which is by no means difficult—or a gathering has been lost at...

The ink which the original scribes used is the usual sepia
colour commonly found in ancient manuscripts. As Tischen-

makes it appear too much of a genuine black. The ink used
by the correctors designated 'A' is the same as that of the original—
doubtless it was the ink which was always used in the <term>scriptorium</term> <note>A dedicated room in a monastery or library for the copying of books.</note>.
The ink used by 'B' is a trifle darker than the original

remained very bright and clear. 'Cc' and 'C*' used a greyer
colour, and the later correctors used black. Red (vermilion)

at the end of Mark. All these are printed in red in Tischen-

->THE SCRIBES AND CORRECTORS<-

The Codex Sinaiticus has been corrected by so many
hands that it affords a most interesting and intricate problem
to the <term>palaeographer</term> <note>A scholar who studies ancient handwriting to date and identify historical documents.</note> who wishes to disentangle the various
stages by which it has reached its present condition, and to
distinguish the different scribes who have contributed to its
development. The task really consists in identifying the
separate writers, beginning with the latest, and ending with
those who seem to have been employed in the original scrip-
torium, and to have been engaged on the preparation of the
manuscript before (if the <term>anachronism</term> <note>The use of a modern concept to describe the past; here, referring to "publishing" a hand-written book.</note> may be permitted) it was
actually published.

The correctors may best be divided into three groups:
(1) The late correctors, probably belonging to the post-
<column-break/>
## Column 2

Caesarean history of the manuscript, and possibly to the monastery
of St. Catherine's on Mt. Sinai. (2) The intermediate correc-
tors, of which certainly the earliest, and probably all, belong to
Caesarea <note>A major center of Christian learning in ancient Palestine.</note>. They are probably not earlier than the fifth nor
later than the seventh century. (3) The early correctors, all
probably belonging to the fourth, and certainly not later than
the fifth century. The earliest of them was engaged on the
manuscript before it left the scriptorium, so that at this point the
question of the correctors passes into that of the original
scribes, and the amount of work which they bestowed on
embellishing the text with <term>superscriptions</term> <note>Headings written at the top of a page.</note>, <term>tituli</term> <note>original Latin: "titles"</note>, and similar
additions.

*The latest correctors.* To these Tischendorf, whose notation
it is convenient to preserve, gave the names of E and D. E is
a quite unimportant scribe who made a very few corrections in
the text, perhaps in the twelfth century, and it is possible that
the same writer added the notes in Greek and Arabic, on
leaves 128 (back) and 130 (front). If E be taken to mean not so much a single
scribe as the latest stage of correction in the manuscript, it may also
be used to designate the writers of a few names scribbled in
the Old Testament—Hilarion, Dionysius, and Theophylact.
Tischendorf thought that E might be regarded as representing
mediaeval monks at St. Catherine's. This is a probable guess,
but, as was stated above, there is no evidence as to the date
when the manuscript was brought to Sinai. D is a scribe of the
eighth century, or later, who restored the writing in the pro-
phetic books, but does not appear to have touched the New
Testament. In Hermas <note>The Shepherd of Hermas, an early Christian literary work included in this Codex.</note>, however, another scribe (D-Hermas) of
much the same date and character added breathings and
accents, and made a few unimportant orthographical changes.
Specimens of D-Hermas and E will be found at the foot of the
third column of Plate II.

*The intermediate correctors.* To these Tischendorf has
given the name of C. Taken together they have done far
more work on the manuscript than any others, and afford extremely
important material for textual criticism; as was shown on
pages vii and following, they represent a Caesarean scriptorium, for one of
them who does not, however, seem to have touched the New
Testament states that he corrected part of the text of the
Old Testament according to the copy of the <term>Hexapla</term> <note>A massive, six-column comparative edition of the Old Testament compiled by the scholar Origen.</note> made
by <term>Pamphilus</term> <note>A Christian scholar and martyr (died 309 AD) who maintained the great library at Caesarea.</note> during his imprisonment, and preserved in the
library at Caesarea.

On the whole the C hands so closely resemble each other,
and can with such little confidence be much separated in date,
that there is considerable force in the suggestion that they all
come from the scriptorium at Caesarea, and represent a
thoroughgoing attempt to accommodate the Codex Sinaiticus
to a model which in the fifth and sixth century was more
fashionable than the original text.

*The early correctors, and original scribes.* The discrimina-
tion of these hands is the most difficult point in the palaeo-
graphical treatment of the MS. The clearest and simplest
way appears to be to break off from the method, which has
hitherto been followed, of starting with the most recent hands,
and to begin by trying to establish the condition of the MS.
when it left the scriptorium.

To the work of the scriptorium, then, obviously belongs the
text itself; so that the first question of all is concerned with
the scribes of the text. After the text comes the 'apparatus'
of the MS.—superscriptions, subscriptions, <term>titles</term> <note>original Latin: "tituli"; the headings of chapters or sections.</note>, paragraph
marks, Ammonian sections, Eusebian canons <note>Ancient systems for numbering and cross-referencing parallel passages in the four Gospels.</note>, and other chap-
ter divisions. These may or may not belong to the scrip-
torium. Finally, it is well known that it was the custom to
submit MSS. to a <term>revision</term> <note>original Greek: "διόρθωσις" (diorthōsis); the formal process of proofreading and correcting a manuscript against its source.</note>, or correction: so that the earliest
corrections may possibly belong to the work of the scriptorium,
and the question is to what extent this can be shown to have
or not to have been the case with the various hands which
seem to have corrected the MS. in the earliest period. Thus
there are three points to discuss. (1) The original scribes,
(2) the 'apparatus', (3) the corrections properly so called.

*The original scribes.* At the first sight the whole Codex seems
to have been written by the same hand ; but a closer inspection
shows that this is erroneous, and according to Tischendorf
four scribes A, B, C, and D were engaged on the text, of

tinguishes the A who wrote part of the New Testament from
the A who wrote the historical books of the Old Testament
and Barnabas, and the B who wrote Isaiah from the B who
wrote Hermas and the other prophetic books. So far as B is
concerned this must remain a question to be discussed in

Codex Sinaiticus. So far as scribe A is concerned, I am unable to see any difference in the handwriting, and in the absence of any such difference, I would hesitate to accept the very minute variations in the treatment of the <term>sacred names</term> <note>original: "nomina sacra"; these are traditional abbreviations used by early Christian scribes for holy names like "God," "Jesus," or "Lord."</note> as sufficient proof of a change in scribe. However, while respecting the opinion of such a distinguished scholar of ancient handwriting, and leaving open the possibility that the Epistle of Barnabas was written by a different hand, it is reasonably clear that scribe A originally wrote all the text of the New Testament except for the Shepherd of Hermas, which was the work of scribe B. Furthermore, scribe D wrote the text on the <term>conjugate leaves</term> <note>Conjugate leaves are pairs of pages formed from a single large sheet of parchment folded in half.</note> (specifically folios 10 and 15, 29 and 30, 88 and 91, and possibly part of folio 126). Examples of these three writing styles—A, B, and D—are displayed side by side in the first three columns of Plate III.

There is perhaps room for reasonable doubt as to whether Tischendorf <note>Constantin von Tischendorf was the 19th-century biblical scholar who discovered the Codex Sinaiticus at Saint Catherine's Monastery.</note> was correct in distinguishing scribe A from scribe B. Personally, however, I fully accept his judgment. After the long acquaintance with scribe A's style required to photograph every page, I felt—while watching the script "appear" on the negative in the developing tray—that the first page of Hermas was different from the others. It seemed to "emerge" differently, even though I did not know which specific plate it was at the time. The same sensation was even more noticeable with the plates belonging to scribe D. 

It would be too much to claim that this purely personal experience should carry great weight for others. I admit that I cannot perfectly analyze the difference between scribes A and B, and the distinction is not as clear to me now as it was when I spent most of every day studying the manuscript. Nevertheless, I believe that if anyone spends time turning over a few leaves of Hermas and then a few leaves of the rest of the New Testament, they will feel a difference in the script. If they focus on the right-hand ends of the lines, they will get the superficial impression that more lines end in the horizontal stroke representing the final letter "N" in Hermas than elsewhere. Detailed analysis shows this is not actually the case—or at least not to a significant degree. The impression is created solely by the fact that these strokes in Hermas are longer and somewhat heavier; instead of being placed partly over the final vowel, they tend to start after it and stretch far into the margin. This is admittedly
->c 2<-
<column-break/>
## Column 2
a minor point, but it helps justify the view that Hermas was written by a different scribe than the rest of the New Testament.

Distinguishing scribe D from scribes A and B is easier and leaves no room for reasonable doubt. There is a clear difference in the handwriting, though it is easier to see than to describe. Perhaps the letters are somewhat squarer in D than in A—the height being smaller in proportion to the width—and D’s writing is generally more attractive than A’s. But the deciding factor is that scribe D constantly fills out the end of a line with a specific mark ( > ), which scribe A or B rarely or never use. A sample column by scribe D is provided in the third column of Plate III.

It was scribe D whom Tischendorf identified as the same person who wrote the New Testament in the Codex Vaticanus <note>Another of the most important 4th-century Greek Bibles, held in the Vatican Library.</note>. A sample of the latter is shown in the fourth column of Plate III; those who compare this with the third column (by scribe D) will likely agree immediately that there is no evidence to support Tischendorf's theory. It is surprising that the sharp eye which detected the subtle differences between A, B, and D—differences anyone else might be forgiven for missing—could ever think for a moment that scribe D’s writing was identical to that of the Codex Vaticanus.

The conjugate leaves written by scribe D are clearly <term>replacement leaves</term> <note>original: "cancel-leaves"; these are pages written after the main manuscript was finished to replace original pages that were damaged or contained too many errors.</note>. That is to say, they were written after the manuscript had been completed to take the place of others (likely written by scribe A) that were somehow imperfect or ruined. Such replacing of rejected leaves would naturally be part of the <term>correction</term> <note>original: "διόρθωσις" (diorthosis); the formal process of proofreading and revising a manuscript in a professional scriptorium.</note> of the manuscript in the workshop. That this was the case is made practically certain by the fact that scribe D also wrote the entire books of Tobit and Judith in the Old Testament, proving he was a regular member of the scriptorium staff. 

The importance of this point is that it shows that any work done on the manuscript before these replacement leaves were added must also be considered work performed within the original scriptorium. It is useful here to list the details for which this can be proven: (a) The Eusebian apparatus <note>A system of numbered sections and tables used to cross-reference similar passages across the four Gospels, created by Eusebius of Caesarea.</note> must have been added before the replacement leaves in Matthew (folios 10 and 15), because these specific leaves—and only these—lack the Section and Canon numbers. Thus, the person who added this cross-referencing system belonged to the original scriptorium. (b) Similar logic shows that the scribe who added the <term>line counts</term> <note>original: "στίχοι" (stichoi); these were counts of lines or verses, often used to measure the length of a work or to pay scribes.</note> in the Epistles also belonged to the scriptorium, for, after the Epistle to—

**The apparatus.** This may be defined as consisting of: 
(1) **Superscriptions** added at the beginning of each book, and afterwards inserted either on each <term>recto</term> <note>The "front" or right-hand page of a leaf.</note>, or distributed on the "open page" between <term>verso</term> <note>The "back" or left-hand page of a leaf.</note> and recto, or, in the Gospels especially, on alternate "open pages." (2) The **subscriptions** at the end of each book. (3) The **Eusebian apparatus** in the Gospels <note>A system of cross-referencing parallel passages across the four Gospels, developed by Eusebius of Caesarea.</note>. (4) The **Paragraph marks** in the Gospels. (5) The **"Euthalian" chapter divisions** in Acts. (6) The <term>chapter headings</term> <note>original: tituli</note> in Acts. (7) The reckoning of <term>lines of text</term> <note>original: στίχοι (stichoi); a standard measure of length used by ancient scribes to calculate payment or book size.</note> at the end of the Epistles.

The questions in each case are whether the scribe belonged to the <term>scriptorium</term> <note>The specialized writing room where the manuscript was produced.</note> or not; if he did, whether he can be identified with the scribe of any other part of the manuscript, and if he did not, to what date he ought to be assigned.

(1) **The superscriptions.** A full selection of these specimens is given in Plate I. It will be easily seen that there is great variation in the style, and that this variation is not regular. The scribe or scribes seem sometimes to write in small and sometimes in large letters on no fixed plan. This creates at first sight the impression of diversity of hands; but further study dispels this view, and leads rather to the conclusion that Tischendorf was right in assigning all the superscriptions to the original scribe D, except those in Hermas, which seem to be by B, the scribe of the text. That the scribe was D rather than A is shown partly by the general impression made on the eye, partly by the fact that the superscriptions are not wanting on the cancel-leaves written by D, where they are precisely similar to those on the other pages, and partly by their resemblance to the subscriptions written by D, and their difference from the subscriptions written by A. 

The most convincing proof that only one hand has been busy with the superscriptions is seen if instead of looking at the specimens given in the order in which they are arranged (that in which they come in the manuscript), they are taken in the order of gradation of change of style. Take for instance the following series:—Luke (29<sup>r</sup>), Mark (18<sup>v</sup>), Matthew (11<sup>v</sup>, 12<sup>r</sup>), Matthew (2<sup>r</sup>), Romans (62<sup>r</sup>), 1 Corinthians (69<sup>r</sup>), 2 Peter (124<sup>r</sup>), Ephesians (82<sup>r</sup>), 1 Thessalonians (87<sup>r</sup>), Colossians (85<sup>v</sup>), Hebrews (92<sup>r</sup>). Is it not impossible to say that any one of these is in a hand other than that of the example preceding or following? Is it

A further conclusion follows from a consideration of the examples given in Plate I. Just as at the top of the series, if it were arranged in order of gradation of style, there would appear specimens in bold <term>uncial</term> <note>A style of script written entirely in capital letters, common in Greek and Latin manuscripts from the 4th to 8th centuries.</note>, resembling closely the ordinary hand of D in the text, so the middle and end of the series supply specimens equally closely resembling the corrector A¹. This suggests that the scribe D is identical with the corrector A¹, and, as will be shown when the correctors are discussed, there is other evidence to corroborate this view.

(2) **The subscriptions.** These afford less room for doubt than the superscriptions. All of them were written by A except those to Mark and 1 Thessalonians, which come on the cancel-leaves written by D. Tischendorf, it is true, also regarded the subscription to John as written by D, together with the whole of the last verse of the Gospel, but an inspection of the subscription (given in Plate I) will probably suggest to most minds that there is on the contrary a close resemblance to the style of A, but not to that of D. Tischendorf argued that there was a change of ink visible at the beginning of the last verse. This is naturally too small a point to be observable in a photograph. My own impression is that the scribe took a fresh dip of ink, and possibly mended his pen, but I can see nothing more, and in general I should have said that A and D used precisely the same ink, and held their pens at precisely the same angle, so that no valid argument can be based on the minute variations of form, which may quite as probably be due to an alteration of posture by the same scribe as to a change of writers.

(3) **The Eusebian apparatus.** This is added in red, by a hand which is shown by the argument given above (page xix) to be anterior to the cancel-leaves of D, and therefore to belong to the scriptorium. to show that probably both were written by the same 
hand, though the scribe varied his ‘stroke’. This passage 
is interesting as suggesting that it was usual in a scriptorium 
for the <term>corrector</term> <note>original: "διορθωτής" (diorthōtēs); a professional reviser who checked the work of the scribes against a master copy.</note> to correct the text before the titles, subscrip-

Dziatzko’s contention that the custom of adding superscrip-
tions began in the second half of the fourth century, and at 
first were not put in by the original scribe (see p. xiii). A 
further illustration of the same point is perhaps afforded by 
the first example classified on Plate II as doubtful. Here 
the scribe who added the Eusebian apparatus <note>A system of cross-referencing parallel passages in the four Gospels, developed by Eusebius of Caesarea.</note> has placed the 
appropriate numerals against a correction in the lower margin. 
It is, however, doubtful whether this correction is from the hand 
of A², and there are in any case two possibilities; (1) that the 
correction was made before the Eusebian scribe did his work, 
(2) that the Eusebian scribe noticed that the beginning of his 
section was missing, and himself added it in the margin, affixing 
the proper number. I am inclined to think that the second is 
the correct view, as the writing of the correction seems to 
me to be identical neither with A² nor with A³, to both of 
which it has superficial resemblance. In this case we have 
in this correction a specimen of the writing of the Eusebian 
scribe: it is doubtful whether there are any others, though it is 
of course possible that some of the many corrections, which 
are too short to enable us to identify the hand, may be due to 
this scribe. 
Tischendorf <note>Constantin von Tischendorf (1815–1874), the German biblical scholar who discovered the Codex Sinaiticus at Saint Catherine's Monastery.</note> thought that he had found a convincing proof 
of the identity of A² with the original scribe D in the cor-
rection to <vocab>Matt. v. 45</vocab> (f. 3ʳ), given in the second column 
of Plate II. Here the large uncial <note>A script consisting entirely of capital letters, common in Greek and Latin manuscripts from the 4th to 8th centuries.</note> ends with the incomplete 
sentence <note>original: "καὶ βρέχει ἐπὶ"</note> **and sends rain on** and the missing words—<note>original: "δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους"</note> **the just and the unjust**—are supplied in smaller letters. The smaller letters 
are certainly in the hand of A², and Tischendorf thought that 
the larger letters are in the hand of D. But there is not, in my 
judgement, any reason for thinking that he was right; there is 
no real difference in the style, and in any case D’s script is so 
nearly the same as A’s that these words afford no means of 
deciding between the two hands. Moreover, his argument that 
no one would break off in the middle of a sentence with **on** <note>original: "ἐπὶ"</note> is

Moreover, it will probably be agreed on the ground of general

and this view is rendered practically certain by the absence of 
the **line-counts** from f. 88, which was written by D. 
It will be convenient at this point to summarize the scribes 
who have so far been shown to have been working in the 
scriptorium, for none of the other early correctors can be 
proved with certainty to have belonged to it. The list is:— 
**Scribe A**, wrote the greater part of the text, and subscrip-
tions. 
**Scribe B**, wrote the Shepherd of Hermas. 
**Scribe D**, wrote the cancel-leaves, and superscriptions. 
**Corrector A¹**, probably identical with scribe D. 
**Corrector A²**, almost certainly identical with scribe D. 
**Scribe E**, the writer of the Eusebian apparatus. 
**Scribe S**, the writer of the **line-counts** <note>original: "στίχοι"</note>. 
All these writers worked on the MS. before it left the 
scriptorium. It is highly probable that the same is true of 
some of those which remain to be considered, but evidence is 
not forthcoming.

corrections have been made by a hand which cannot for any 
palaeographical reasons be regarded as later than A², but is 
clearly distinct from it. It is not marked by any alternation 
of size in the letters, or by the curious <note>original: "δ" (delta)</note> **delta** of A², and is much

## Column 1
