Possibly this scribe belonged to the scriptorium <note>A specialized room in a monastery or library for the copying and correcting of manuscripts.</note>, but there is no definite proof that such was the case, unless it be thought that he was the scribe of the correction to which the Eusebian scribe affixed the number (see above, and cf. the first of the ‘doubtful’ examples in Plate II). At one time I was inclined to think that this was so, on the ground of the ‘monogram’ in this correction, but further consideration has made me think that this is probably not the case. Thus it remains uncertain whether A¹ belonged to the scriptorium or should be regarded as one of the earliest hands who touched the manuscript after it had been ‘issued’. Examples are given in the second column of Plate II.

*The corrector A⁴.* There are only a very few corrections by this hand. It probably belongs to the fourth century, but according to Dr. Kenyon’s judgement might possibly be a little later than the scribes hitherto mentioned. It is marked by an extreme regularity and neatness (see the fourth column of Plate II).

*The corrector A⁵.* This scribe, easily distinguished by his graceful style, and the curious shape of his <term>x</term> <note>original: "ξ" (xi); the Greek letter corresponding to the English 'x'.</note>, only made a few corrections. He is no doubt contemporary with the manuscript or nearly so, but there is nothing to show whether he did or did not belong to the scriptorium. Examples are given in the third column of Plate II.

*A-Herm.* Possibly distinct from all the other A-group correctors is one who seems to have acted as the <term>corrector</term> <note>original: "διορθωτής" (diorthōtēs); a professional reviser who checked the scribe's work for accuracy.</note> of the *Shepherd of Hermas* <note>An early Christian literary work that was included at the end of the Codex Sinaiticus.</note> in a small delicate hand. Examples are given in the third column of Plate II.

All the scribes hitherto dealt with belong to the A-group which Tischendorf <note>Constantin von Tischendorf (1815–1874), the German biblical scholar who discovered the Codex Sinaiticus at St. Catherine's Monastery.</note> regarded as belonging to the scriptorium. In some places he expressed himself in such a way as to give the impression that he meant A—the <term>aleph</term> <note>original: "ℵ"; the Hebrew letter used as the symbol for Codex Sinaiticus in textual criticism.</note> of the critical Greek Testament—to refer to a single scribe. This he certainly did not really think, and he only omitted to define the facts more clearly because it is so often impossible to say to which of the group any given correction belongs, even though it is plain that it is not to be assigned to any later hand.

Outside the pure A family come the scribes known as A-oblique, B, and B-a. They differ from those which have been already treated in that they probably do not belong to the scriptorium. They are, however, not much later than the

<column-break/>

## Column 2

A group—the fifth century is the latest date to which they can be assigned—and they may be regarded as representing the corrections of some of the earliest owners of the Codex.

*The corrector A-oblique.* This scribe, who, as his title suggests, used sloping characters, is quite unimportant. He only made a few casual alterations; Tischendorf only classed him in the A group because his is a clearly early hand, and he used ink which is indistinguishable from that of the A-group correctors. Specimens of his script can be seen in the fourth column of Plate II.

*The corrector B.* Far more interest attaches to the work of this scribe, whose writing is chiefly distinguishable from the A group by a slight difference of tint, which is not discernible in a photograph. He was contemporary with the A group or nearly so, and was chiefly interested in small points of spelling and scholarship. On the first pages of Matthew he made frequent corrections which are very important for the history of the orthographical <note>Relating to spelling conventions.</note> tradition as to proper names, but his interest soon declined, and his hand is not found outside the first Gospel. He may very well have been a scholarly owner, who had strong opinions as to the proper way of spelling the names of the Patriarchs and Kings of Israel. Tischendorf gives a full list of the corrections; it is exceedingly difficult to see them either in the facsimile or in the manuscript, but there is not, I believe, any reason for doubting the correctness of his judgement. With great trouble I succeeded in verifying in the manuscript all the corrections which Tischendorf indicates on leaf 1. So far as I can judge the facsimile is not more obscure than the manuscript, except in so far as in a manuscript the sense of touch often helps to detect erasures, or the erosions of faded ink, and this is of course impossible in a photographic facsimile. It may, however, be thought with some probability that the manuscript was in a better condition when Tischendorf first saw it than now. The Imperial Library at St. Petersburg is no doubt in every other respect an infinitely better home for a manuscript than the convent of St. Catherine, but on the important matter of climate one may suspect that the advantage is with Sinai. Specimens of B are given in the third column of Plate II.

*The corrector B-a.* This symbol was used by Tischendorf to indicate a few corrections in a hand which cannot with certainty be identified either with B or with any of the A group.

The following table may perhaps be useful as a summary of the results, with regard to the origin, creation, and history of the manuscript, which the foregoing discussion has rendered probable:

**4th Century <note>original: "Saec. IV"</note>. In a scribal workshop <note>original: "scriptorium"</note> in Egypt.**
> Scribe A wrote the New Testament including the concluding notes <note>original: "Subscriptions"</note>, Scribe B wrote the Shepherd of Hermas <note>original: "Hermas"</note>, Scribe E added the Eusebian cross-reference system <note>original: "Eusebian Apparatus"</note>, and Scribe S added the <term>line counts</term> <note>original: "στίχοι" (stichoi); measurements of the text's length used for payment or verification.</note> to the Epistles. Scribe D (the same as corrector A¹ and possibly A²) added the titles at the beginning of books, and probably the <term>headings</term> <note>original: "tituli"; chapter summaries or titles.</note> in the book of Acts. He also wrote <term>replacement pages</term> <note>original: "cancel-leaves"; new pages substituted for original ones that had errors.</note> for eight sheets, and (using

<column-break/>

> a smaller and different type of handwriting when necessary) acted as the <term>Chief Editor</term> <note>original: "Diorthotes"; the professional proofreader or supervisor of a scriptorium.</note> of the whole manuscript. He omitted to do the work of scribes E and S on the replacement pages. The rest of the ‘A’ group of correctors probably also belong to this period and place, but this is uncertain.

**4th–5th Century <note>original: "Saec. IV–V"</note>. In a locality which is unknown.**
> Scribes B, B², and "A-slanting" <note>original: "A^obliq"</note>, and possibly some of the doubtful members of the A group, worked on the manuscript; whether they were in the same or another scribal workshop cannot be determined.

**5th–7th Century <note>original: "Saec. V–VII"</note>. In the monastery at Caesarea.**
> The manuscript was corrected by the group of "C" correctors (specifically Cᵃ, Cᵇ, Cᶜ, Cᶜ*, and the Pamphilian corrector Cᴾᵃᵐᵖʰ), and possibly others.

**8th–12th Century <note>original: "Saec. VIII–XII"</note>. Possibly on Mount Sinai.**
> At least two correctors, designated D and E, made unimportant and fortunately few corrections.

## Column 1
-> Codex Vaticanus <-
<note>This column features the Book of Acts (11:28–12:5) from the Codex Vaticanus, one of the oldest and most complete Greek bibles.</note>

...But one of them named Agabus stood up and signaled through the <term>Spirit (PNA)</term> <note>original: "Πνεύματος" (Pneumatos), here abbreviated as a sacred name (nomen sacrum).</note> that a great famine was about to come upon the whole world, which indeed happened during the time of Claudius. And the disciples, according to how each was prospering, determined each of them to send a contribution for service to the brothers living in Judea. This they also did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul. About that time, King Herod laid hands on some of those from the church to mistreat them. He killed James, the brother of John, with a sword. And seeing that it was pleasing to the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter as well. These were the days of Unleavened Bread. Having seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. So Peter was kept in the prison, but earnest prayer was being made by the church concerning him to <term>God (THN)</term> <note>original: "Θεόν" (Theon).</note>...

## Column 2
-> Scribe D <-
<note>Scribe D is one of the main scribes of Codex Sinaiticus, known for a very regular, professional uncial script. This passage is from 1 Thessalonians 5:3–11.</note>

...Whenever they say "peace and security," then sudden destruction comes upon them just as labor pains upon a woman who is pregnant, and they will certainly not escape. But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that the day should overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night nor of darkness. So then, let us not sleep as the others do, but let us be watchful and sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk are drunk at night. But we, being of the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet <margin>of salvation (rias)</margin> <note>The letters "rias" were added in the margin to complete the word "soterias" (of salvation).</note> the hope of salvation. For <term>God (THS)</term> <note>original: "Θεός" (Theos).</note> did not appoint us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation through our <term>Lord (KY)</term> <note>original: "Κυρίου" (Kyriou).</note> <term>Jesus (IY)</term> <note>original: "Ἰησοῦ" (Iēsou).</note> <term>Christ (XY)</term> <note>original: "Χριστοῦ" (Christou)</note> who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep, we might live together with him. Therefore, encourage one another.

## Column 4

Masters, provide justice and equality to your servants, knowing that you also have <margin>the</margin> <note>The marginal "τη" (te) likely serves as a correction or reference mark.</note> a <term>Lord (KN)</term> <note>original: "Κύριον" (Kyrion).</note> in heaven. Walk in wisdom toward those outside, making the most of the time. Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, to know how it is necessary for you to answer each one. Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the <term>Lord (KO)</term> <note>original: "Κυρίῳ" (Kyriō).</note>, will make known to you all my affairs. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know the things concerning us and that he may encourage your hearts, along with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you all the things here.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page (Folio 8 recto/207), Jesus concludes a warning about unclean spirits and begins a series of teachings known as the "Parables of the Kingdom." This page contains the famous parables of the Sower, the Weeds, the Mustard Seed, and the Leaven, along with Jesus's private explanation to his disciples. The marginal numbers (135–139) refer to the Eusebian Canons, an early system for cross-referencing parallel passages in the four Gospels.</meta>

But the one sown on the rocky places, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself but is temporary, and when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, immediately he falls away.

--- Page 65 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Olivet Discourse," shifting from signs of the end of the age to parables of watchfulness and readiness. The previous page discussed the "abomination of desolation" and the visible signs of the Son of Man's coming. Here, the focus turns to the unpredictable timing of these events and the necessity of being prepared, using the examples of Noah, a homeowner, two types of servants, ten virgins, and the distribution of talents.</meta>

<meta>This page marks the transition from the Gospel of Matthew to the Gospel of Mark. The scribe begins Mark on a new column with a decorative headpiece. The text is written in uncial script with "Nomina Sacra" (abbreviated sacred names). Notably, the phrase "Son of God" in the first verse appears to be a later correction or addition, as it is squeezed above the main line of text.</meta>

<summary>This page of the Codex Sinaiticus preserves Luke 6:19–45, covering the end of Jesus's healing of the crowd, the four Beatitudes and four Woes of Luke's "Sermon on the Plain," the commands to love enemies and practice the Golden Rule, and a series of vivid parables about judgment, blind guides, trees and their fruit, and the heart's overflow. It is a foundational passage of early Christian ethical teaching and offers important textual evidence from one of the oldest surviving complete New Testament manuscripts.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the Gospel of John, following the conclusion of the Gospel of Luke. While Luke ended with the earthly departure of Jesus (the Ascension), John begins by looking back before time itself to the nature of the "Word." This specific manuscript is a famous 4th-century witness (Codex Sinaiticus) known for its distinct phrasing in the opening chapter.</meta>

--- Page 163 ---
<meta>This page continues the Apostle Paul's Letter to the Romans. While the previous page discussed the faith of Abraham and how he was credited with righteousness before the Law was given, this page transitions into the second half of Chapter 5 and the whole of Chapter 6. Here, Paul compares the "first man" Adam with the "second man" Christ, arguing that just as one man's sin brought death, one man's act of righteousness brings life. He then addresses the ethical question: if grace is so abundant, should we keep sinning? Paul answers with a firm 'no,' explaining that baptism unites a person with Christ's death and resurrection, making them "slaves to righteousness" rather than "slaves to sin."</meta>

# FIRST TO THE CORINTHIANS

## Column 1

...to those of us being saved, it is the power of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term>. 
For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and the discernment of the discerning I will set aside. 
Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? 
Has not <term>God (original: ΘΣ)</term> made foolish the wisdom of this world? 
For since, in the wisdom of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term>, the world did not know <term>God (original: ΘΝ)</term> through its own wisdom, <term>God (original: ΘΣ)</term> was well-pleased through the foolishness of the message preached to save those who believe. 
Since both Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom; 
but we preach <term>Christ (original: ΧΝ)</term> crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to the nations, 
but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, <term>Christ (original: ΧΝ)</term> is the power of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term> and the wisdom of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term>; 
because the foolishness of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term> is wiser than men, and the weakness of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term> is stronger than men <note>original: "is" (added by a scribe for grammatical completeness)</note>.

# FIRST TO THE CORINTHIANS

# FIRST TO THE CORINTHIANS

## Column 1

in <term>Christ (original: ΧΩ)</term> <term>Jesus (original: ΙΥ)</term> through the gospel I fathered you. I urge you then, be imitators of me. For this reason I sent to you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful child in the <term>Lord (original: ΚΩ)</term>, who will remind you of my ways in <term>Christ (original: ΧΩ)</term> <term>Jesus (original: ΙΥ)</term>, just as I teach everywhere in every church. 

Now some have become puffed up <note>The Greek term implies being arrogant or conceited, like a bellows filled with air.</note>, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you quickly, if the <term>Lord (original: ΚΣ)</term> wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up but their power. For the kingdom of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term> is not in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod <note>A staff used for discipline or correction.</note>, or in love and a spirit of gentleness? 

It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not even found among the pagans: that a man has his <term>father's (original: ΠΡΣ)</term> wife. And you are puffed up! Should you not rather have mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from among you?

<column-break/>

## Column 2

For though I am absent in body, I am present in <term>Spirit (original: ΠΝΙ)</term>; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who has done such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the <term>Lord (original: ΚΥ)</term> <term>Jesus (original: ΙΥ)</term> <term>Christ (original: ΧΥ)</term>, and my spirit is present with the power of our <term>Lord (original: ΚΥ)</term> <term>Jesus (original: ΙΥ)</term>, you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his <term>spirit (original: ΠΝΑ)</term> may be saved in the day of the <term>Lord (original: ΚΥ)</term> <term>Jesus (original: ΙΥ)</term>. 

Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough? Clean out the old yeast so that you may be a new batch, just as you really are unleavened. 

For <term>Christ (original: ΧΣ)</term>, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the festival, not with the old yeast, the yeast of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. 

I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.

<column-break/>

## Column 3

But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is sexually immoral or greedy, or an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one. 

For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? <term>God (original: ΘΣ)</term> judges those outside. Purge the evil person from among yourselves. 

Does any one of you, when he has a grievance against another, dare to go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints? <note>Paul uses "saints" to refer to the members of the Christian community.</note> Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases? 

Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life! So if you have such cases, do you appoint as judges those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers? But brother goes to court against...

<column-break/>

## Column 4

...brother, and that before unbelievers? 

To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—and even your own brothers! 

Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term>? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality <note>The Greek uses two terms here, 'malakoi' and 'arsenokoitai,' referring to passive and active roles in same-sex acts in a Greco-Roman context.</note>, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term>. 

And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the <term>Lord (original: ΚΥ)</term> <term>Jesus (original: ΙΥ)</term> <term>Christ (original: ΧΥ)</term> and by the <term>Spirit (original: ΠΝΙ)</term> of our <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term>. 

"All things are lawful for me," but not all things are helpful. "All things are lawful for me," but I will not be dominated by anything. "Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food"—and <term>God (original: ΘΣ)</term> will destroy both one and the other.

## Column 1

The body however is not for sexual immorality but for the <term>Lord (original: ΚΩ)</term>, and the <term>Lord (original: ΚΣ)</term> for the body; and <term>God (original: ΘΣ)</term> both raised the <term>Lord (original: ΚΝ)</term> and will raise us up through his power. 

Do you not know that your bodies are members of <term>Christ (original: ΧΥ)</term>? Shall I then take the members of <term>Christ (original: ΧΥ)</term> and make them members of a prostitute? Never! Or do you not know that the one who joins himself to a prostitute is one body with her? For it says, "The two shall become one flesh." But the one who joins himself to the <term>Lord (original: ΚΩ)</term> is one <term>Spirit (original: ΠΝΑ)</term> with him. 

Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the person who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body. Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy <term>Spirit (original: ΠΝΣ)</term> within you, whom you have from <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term>? And you are not your own. ## Column 3

let her remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband—and the husband should not divorce his wife.

To the rest I say, I and not the <term>Lord (original: ΚΣ)</term>: If any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him. For the unbelieving husband is made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy through the brother <note>original: ἀδελφῷ; some manuscripts read "husband" here to match the parallel structure.</note>. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy. 

But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. <term>God (original: ΘΣ)</term> has called you to peace. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? 

Only let each person lead the life that the <term>Lord (original: ΚΣ)</term> has assigned to him, and to which <term>God (original: ΘΣ)</term> has called him. This is my rule in all the churches.

## Column 4

Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. 

Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of <term>God (original: ΘΥ)</term> is everything. Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. 

Were you a slave when called? Do not let it concern you. But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity. For he who was called in the <term>Lord (original: ΚΩ)</term> as a slave is a freedperson of the <term>Lord (original: ΚΥ)</term>. Likewise he who was free when called is a slave of <term>Christ (original: ΧΥ)</term>. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with <term>God (original: ΘΩ)</term>.

Now concerning virgins, I have no command from the <term>Lord (original: ΚΥ)</term>, but I give my opinion as one who by the <term>Lord's (original: ΚΥ)</term> mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress <note>Likely referring to a period of persecution or social upheaval facing the early Christians.</note> it is good for a person to remain as he is. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.

## Column 1

And Barnabas—do we not have the right to refrain from working for a living? <margin>Section 1</margin> Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not drink the milk of the flock?

Do I say these things only on <term>human authority</term> <note>original: ΑΝΟΝ, a *nomen sacrum* (sacred abbreviation) for *anthrōpon*, meaning "human" or "man"</note>? If we have sown <term>spiritual things</term> <note>original: ΠΝΙΚΑ, abbreviation for *pneumatika*</note> among you, <margin>Section 13</margin> is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim over you, do not we still more?

## Column 2

-tar share in what is sacrificed on the altar? In the same way, the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: ΚΣ, *nomen sacrum* for *Kyrios*</note> commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.

But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing this so that they may be applied in my case. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. 

If I proclaim the gospel, this gives me no ground for boasting, for an obligation is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel! For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward; but if not of my own will, I am entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? Just this: that in my proclamation I may make the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my rights in the gospel.

For though I am free from all, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law—

## Column 3

—though I myself am not under the law—so that I might win those under the law. To the weak I became weak, so that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some. and if the hand should say, "Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body," it is not for this reason any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, "Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body," it is not for this reason any less a part of the body. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? ## Column 3

If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become a sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. And if I give away all my possessions, and if I deliver up my body so that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing. 

<margin>114</margin> Love is patient, love is kind, it does not envy, love does not brag, it is not arrogant, it does not act unbecomingly, it does not seek its own, it is not provoked, it does not keep a record of wrongs, it does not rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails. 

But if there are prophecies, they will be done away with; if there are tongues, they will cease; if there is knowledge, it will be done away with. For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away with. When I was a child,

## Column 1

...greater <note>The text begins mid-sentence, completing the thought that the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues</note> unless he interprets, so that the church may receive building up. 

Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I speak to you by way of revelation, or knowledge, or prophecy, or teaching? Even lifeless things that produce a sound—whether a flute or a harp—if they do not give a distinction in the tones, how will what is played on the flute or the harp be recognized? For indeed, if the trumpet gives an unclear sound, who will prepare for battle? 

In the same way, if you do not produce intelligible speech with your tongue, how will what is spoken be known? For you will be speaking into the air. There are, perhaps, many kinds of languages in the world, and none is without meaning. If, then, I do not know the power of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker, and the speaker will be a foreigner to me. 

So also you, since you are zealous for <term>spiritual gifts</term> <note>original: ΠΝΑΤΩΝ (*pneumatōn*), a *nomen sacrum* referring here to spiritual manifestations or spirits</note>, seek to abound in them for the

# SECOND TO THE CORINTHIANS

## Column 1

...to prepare this blessing. I thought it necessary, therefore, to urge the brothers that they should go on ahead to you and arrange in advance your previously promised blessing, so that this might be ready as a blessing and not as a matter of greed.

This is the point: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and the one who sows with blessings will also reap with blessings. Each one should give just as he has decided in his heart, not out of regret or out of necessity; for <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΣ (*Theos*) — a "sacred name" abbreviation for God.</note> loves a cheerful <note>The scribe originally omitted the ending of the word "cheerful" (*hilaron*), writing only *hila-*. This is a common "slip of the pen" in ancient manuscripts.</note> giver.

And <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΣ (*Theos*)</note> is able to make every grace abound to you, so that in everything, always having all sufficiency, you may abound in every good work, just as it is written:
“He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains forever.” <note>This is a quotation from Psalm 112:9, illustrating the enduring nature of generosity.</note>

Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the harvest of your

<column-break/>

## Column 2

righteousness. You will be enriched in every way for all sincerity, which produces thanksgiving to <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΩ (*Theo*)</note> through us; because the ministry of this service is not only fully supplying the needs of the saints, but is also abounding through many thanksgivings to <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΩ (*Theo*)</note>. 

Through the proof of this ministry, they glorify <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΝ (*Theon*)</note> for the obedience of your confession to the gospel of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note> and for the sincerity of your fellowship toward them and toward everyone. And in their prayer for you, they long for you because of the surpassing grace of <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (*Theou*)</note> upon you. Thanks be to <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΩ (*Theo*)</note> for his indescribable gift!

Now I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the gentleness and kindness of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>—I who am "humble" when face to face among you, but "bold" toward you when away! I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to be bold with the confidence with which I propose to show

<column-break/>

## Column 3

daring against some who consider us as walking according to the flesh. 

For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful to <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΩ (*Theo*)</note> for the tearing down of strongholds. We are tearing down arguments and every high thing that lifts itself up against the knowledge of <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (*Theou*)</note>, and taking every thought captive to the obedience of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>, and being ready to punish every disobedience, whenever your obedience is complete.

Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident in himself that he belongs to <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>, <margin>21</margin> let him consider this again for himself: that just as he belongs to <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>, so also do we. For even if I should boast somewhat more about our authority, which the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: ΚΣ (*Kyrios*)</note> gave for building you up and not for tearing you down, I will not be ashamed. 

I do not want to seem as if I am trying to frighten you through my letters; for "the letters," someone says, "are weighty and strong, but his bodily

<column-break/>

## Column 4

presence is weak and his speech is contemptible." Let such a person consider this: that what we are in word through letters when absent, we will also be in deed when present.

For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves; but they, when they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, do not understand.

We, however, will not boast beyond limits, but according to the measure of the rule <note>original: κανόνος (*kanonos*) — the "canon" or standard/boundary line God assigned to Paul's mission.</note> which <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΣ (*Theos*)</note> assigned to us as a measure, to reach even as far as you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as if we did not reach you; for we were the first to come all the way to you in the gospel of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>. We do not boast beyond limits in the labors of others, but we have the hope that as your faith increases, we shall be greatly enlarged among you according to our rule, so that we may preach the gospel in the regions beyond you, and not boast in someone else’s rule...

# TO THE CORINTHIANS II

## Column 1

...in order to boast in things already prepared by others.
But "let the one who boasts, boast in the <term>Lord</term>" <note>original: ΚΩ (*Kyrio*) — a shortened "sacred name" (Nomen Sacrum) for the Lord.</note>.
For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: ΚΣ (*Kyrios*)</note> commends.

I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness; but indeed, do bear with me.
For I am jealous for you with a jealousy of <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (*Theou*)</note>, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΩ (*Christo*)</note>.
But I fear lest somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, your thoughts should be corrupted from the simplicity and purity that is toward <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΝ (*Christon*)</note>.

For if the one who comes preaches another <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: ΙΝ (*Iesoun*)</note> whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different spirit which you did not receive, or a different gospel which you did not accept, you bear with it well enough!
For I consider myself to be in no way inferior to those "super-apostles."
Even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this clear to you in all things.
Or did I commit a sin...

<column-break/>

## Column 2

...by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached the gospel of <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (*Theou*)</note> to you free of charge?
I robbed other churches by taking support <note>original: ὀψώνιον (*opsonion*) — literally "rations" or "wages," often used for a soldier's pay.</note> from them for my service to you.
And when I was present with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need.
And in everything I kept myself from being a burden to you, and I will continue to do so.

As the truth of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note> is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia <note>The Roman province where Corinth was located.</note>.
Why? Because I do not love you? <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΣ (*Theos*)</note> knows I do!
And what I do I will continue to do, so that I may cut off the opportunity of those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things they boast about.

For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>.
And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.
It is no great thing then if also his...

<column-break/>

## Column 3

...ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works.
Again I say, let no one think me a fool; but if you do, then accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.
What I am saying in this boastful confidence, I say not according to the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: ΚΝ (*Kyrion*)</note> but as a fool.

Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
For you gladly bear with fools, being so wise yourselves!
For you bear it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes advantage of you, if someone puts on airs, if someone strikes you in the face.
To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!

But in whatever anyone else dares to boast—I am speaking as a fool—I also dare to boast.
Are they Hebrews? So am I.
Are they Israelites? So am I.
Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.
Are they ministers of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>?—I am talking like a madman—I am more so: in far more labors, in far more beatings, in far more imprisonments...

<column-break/>

## Column 4

<margin>226</margin> <note>This number likely refers to the page or leaf count in the original codex.</note>
...exceedingly, often near death.
Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one <note>Jewish law limited lashes to forty; one was subtracted to ensure the limit was never accidentally exceeded.</note>.
Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked, a night and a day I have spent in the deep.

In journeys often, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and nakedness.
Apart from these external things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.

Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn with indignation?
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
The <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΣ (*Theos*)</note> and <term>Father</term> <note>original: ΠΗΡ (*Pater*)</note> of the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: ΚΥ (*Kyriou*)</note> <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: ΙΥ (*Iesou*)</note> knows, he who is blessed forever, that I am not lying.
In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize... <note>The text ends mid-word: πιά- (pia-) for πιάσαι (piasai), "to seize."</note>

<summary>Paul defends his apostolic authority by contrasting his own hardships and self-sacrifice with the behavior of "super-apostles." He lists his extensive sufferings, including beatings, shipwrecks, and constant dangers, as the true evidence of his ministry.</summary>

## Column 1

...of the Damascenes, wanting to seize me; and through a window in a basket I was lowered through the wall and escaped his hands.

<meta>This page concludes the Second Epistle to the Corinthians and marks the beginning of the Epistle to the Galatians. It picks up at the final exhortations of Paul to the Corinthian community before transitioning into a stern defense of his apostolic authority to the churches in Galatia.</meta>

## Column 1

Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Or do you not realize about yourselves that <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: ΙΣ (*Iesous*)</note> <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΣ (*Christos*)</note> is in you?—unless indeed you fail the test. 
But I hope that you will realize that we have not failed the test. 
Now we pray to <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΝ (*Theon*)</note> that you do nothing wrong—not so that we may appear to have passed the test, but so that you may do what is right, even if we should seem to have failed. 
For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. 
For we rejoice when we are weak, but you are strong; this is what we pray for: your restoration <note>original: κατάρτισιν (*katartisin*) — refers to being "made complete" or "fully equipped."</note>. 
For this reason I write these things while I am away, so that when I am present I may not have to be severe in using the authority which the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: ΚΣ (*Kyrios*)</note> gave me for building up and not for tearing down. 
Finally, brothers, rejoice, be restored, be encouraged, be of the same mind, live in peace; and the <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΣ (*Theos*)</note> of love and peace will be with you. 
Greet one another with a holy kiss. 
All the saints <note>The term "saints" here refers to the fellow members of the early Christian community.</note> greet you. 

<column-break/>

## Column 2

The grace of the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: ΚΥ (*Kyriou*)</note> <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: ΙΥ (*Iesou*)</note> <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note> and the love of <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (*Theou*)</note> and the fellowship of the Holy <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: ΠΝΣ (*Pneumatos*)</note> be with you all.

## Column 3

Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through a human being, but through <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: ΙΥ (*Iesou*)</note> <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note> and <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (*Theou*)</note> the <term>Father</term> <note>original: ΠΡΣ (*Patros*)</note> who raised him from the dead—and all the brothers with me, to the churches of Galatia: 
Grace to you and peace from <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (*Theou*)</note> our <term>Father</term> <note>original: ΠΡΣ (*Patros*)</note> and the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: ΚΥ (*Kyriou*)</note> <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: ΙΥ (*Iesou*)</note> <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>, who gave himself for our sins, so that he might rescue us from this present evil age according to the will of our <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΥ (*Theou*)</note> and <term>Father</term> <note>original: ΠΡΣ (*Patros*)</note>, to whom be the glory forever and ever; amen. 
I am amazed that you are so quickly turning away from the one who called you in the grace of Christ to a different gospel—which is not another gospel; except there are some who trouble you and want to pervert the gospel of Christ. 
But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let them be accursed <note>original: ἀνάθεμα (*anathema*) — a formal curse or excommunication.</note>. 
As we have said before, and now I say again, if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let them be accursed. 
For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of <term>God</term> <note>original: ΘΝ (*Theon*)</note>? Or am I...

## Column 4

...seeking to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>. 
For I make known to you, brothers, the gospel preached by me, that it is not of human origin; for I did not receive it from a human being, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: ΙΥ (*Iesou*)</note> <term>Christ</term> <note>original: ΧΥ (*Christou*)</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the Epistle to the Galatians with Paul's famous "fruit of the Spirit" list and his personal signature, then opens the Epistle to the Ephesians with a grand liturgical blessing. It is a key witness to the textual history of Ephesians, as the original scribe omitted the words "in Ephesus," reflecting the letter's likely origin as a circular encyclical.</summary>

<summary>This page argues for the superiority of Jesus' priesthood over the Levitical system by comparing him to Melchizedek, an eternal figure without genealogy who received tithes from Abraham. It concludes that Jesus' indestructible life and God's divine oath establish a permanent, perfect covenant that replaces the old law.</summary>

It concludes that Christ's single sacrifice of his own body effectively replaces the old system, fulfilling God's will and providing permanent sanctification.</summary>

The previous page ended with Paul's final instructions and greetings to his protege Timothy. Here, we see the formal closing of that letter followed by the introductory greeting and early instructions for Titus, another of Paul's companions who was overseeing the churches on the island of Crete.</meta>

--- Page 234 ---
<meta>This page represents a transition in the manuscript collection from the personal letters of Paul (specifically the end of Philemon found on the previous page) to the Gospel of Matthew. The fragment consists of a vertical strip from a codex, where the left margin has been lost, requiring the reconstruction of the first few letters of each line. The text is written in an uncial script—an early form of Greek majuscule or capital letters—and uses "Nomina Sacra," which are traditional abbreviations for sacred names like "Lord" and "God."</meta>

<margin>Section 94 (94)</margin> "...having done nothing against the people or the ancestral customs, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. For this reason, therefore, I have requested to see you and speak with you; for it is because of the hope of Israel <note>The "hope of Israel" refers to the long-awaited arrival of the Messiah.</note> that I am bound with this chain." --- Page 288 ---
<meta>This page marks a major transition in the manuscript from the General Epistles (ending with the Epistle of Jude on the previous page) to the Book of Revelation, also known as the Apocalypse of John. The scribe has used a distinct header and centered titles to signify this new section. The text is written in uncial script—an early form of Greek capital letters—and utilizes "Nomina Sacra," which are abbreviated forms of sacred names like "Jesus," "God," and "Lord."</meta>

The law of our <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "ΚΥ" (Kyriou)</note> <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: "ΙΥ" (Iesou)</note> <term>Christ</term> <note>original: "ΧΥ" (Christou)</note>, being without a yoke of necessity, should not have a man-made offering. The previous page established Jesus as the one who appeared in the flesh to fulfill the promises and prepare a "new people" through his suffering. This page transitions into "typology"—an early Christian method of interpreting the Old Testament where events like the Day of Atonement and the sacrifice of the Red Heifer are seen as hidden symbols (types) that prefigure the life and death of Jesus.</meta>

## Column 2

...heart. But you will say: "And yet the people have been circumcised for a seal." But every Syrian and Arab and all the priests of the idols are also circumcised; are they then also part of the covenant? Even the Egyptians are in circumcision.
Learn then, children of love, about all things abundantly: that Abraham, who first gave circumcision, circumcised while looking forward in <term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "ΠΝΙ" (Pneuma).</note> to the <term>Son</term> <note>A correction mark appears above "ΥΝ" (Uion), the abbreviation for Son.</note>, having received the doctrines of three letters. For it says: "And Abraham circumcised eighteen and three hundred men of his household."
What, then, was the knowledge <note>original: "gnōsis" (spiritual insight).</note> given to him? Learn that he mentions the "eighteen" first, and then, after an interval, the "three hundred." As for the "eighteen," *Iota* is ten and *Eta* is eight; there you have <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: "ΙΗ" (the first two letters of Iēsous). In Greek gematria, letters also represent numbers: I = 10, H = 8.</note>. And because the cross in the letter *Tau* was destined to have grace, he also says "three hundred" <note>In Greek, the letter Tau (T) represents the number 300 and was seen by early Christians as a symbol of the cross.</note>. He reveals <term>Jesus</term> in the two letters, and the <term>Cross</term> <note>original: "ΣΡΟΝ" (Stauron).</note> in the one. He who placed the engrafted gift of his teaching within us knows this. No one has learned a more excellent word from me, but I know that you are worthy.

<column-break/>

## Column 3

...from me. But I know that you are worthy.
And because Moses said: "You shall not eat pig, nor eagle, nor hawk, nor raven, nor any fish that does not have scales on itself," he received three doctrines in his understanding. For he says to them in Deuteronomy: "And I will make a covenant of my ordinances with this people." Therefore, it is not a commandment of <term>God</term> to literally not eat; rather, Moses spoke in the <term>Spirit</term>.
Regarding the "pig," he meant this: You shall not associate, he says, with such men who are like pigs. For when they live in luxury, they forget the <term>Lord</term>, but when they are in want, they acknowledge the <term>Lord</term>—just as the pig, when it eats, does not know its master, but when it is hungry, it cries out, and having received food, is silent again.
"Neither shall you eat," he says, "the eagle, nor the hawk, nor the kite, nor the raven." You shall not associate...

<column-break/>

## Column 4

...nor, he says, shall you become like such men, who do not know how to provide food for themselves through labor and sweat, but seize the things of others in their lawlessness; and while they walk in apparent innocence, they are watching to see whom they may plunder because of their greed. Just as <margin>through labor</margin> these birds alone do not provide food for themselves, but sitting idle, they seek how they may eat the flesh of others, being pests in their wickedness.
"And you shall not eat," he says, "the lamprey, nor the octopus, nor the cuttlefish." You shall not, he says, become like such men, who are ungodly to the end and are already condemned to death—just as these little fish alone are cursed and swim in the depths, not swimming on the surface like the rest, but dwelling in the mud at the bottom of the deep.

<summary>This page argues that the true covenant belongs to Christians through Jesus's redemption and presents a "chiliastic" (millennial) view of history, where 6,000 years of human history are followed by a 1,000-year rest. It justifies Christian worship on the "eighth day" (Sunday) rather than the Jewish Sabbath, linking it to the Resurrection.</summary>

Following this, an elderly woman (representing the Church) appears to him while he is in a state of despair over his spiritual condition.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the modern scholarly index provided on the previous page back to the primary ancient text of the Codex Sinaiticus. We are looking at a portion of "The Shepherd of Hermas," specifically the "Mandates" (Commandments). This section, Mandate 4, deals with the early Christian understanding of sin, divorce, and the "second chance" for repentance.</meta>

## Column 1

...or does great wrong for a long time. It seemed, therefore, that there is repentance because of the repentance; not for all <term>men</term> <note>original: ANOS, an abbreviation for anthrōpos</note> will there be the same release for the dead; for he is truly the cause, he says. It is right that his [time] should not be twenty <note>original: eikas, likely referring to a specific count or period of time</note> and all the names he might make for the nations. No, but so that such sexual immorality <note>original manuscript spelling: pornian</note> remains. In repentance, then, so that if [one] of <term>the Lord</term> <note>original: KY, a nomina sacra abbreviation for Kyriou</note> shall live for Him. But if also sexual immorality <note>original manuscript spelling: pornian</note>... nor do you stand of yourself speaking and staying for themselves. Whoever is able to be told to another, these [people]. And it seems, he said, I do not give an opportunity. This <margin>action</margin> <note>a marginal correction completes the word as praxis, meaning deed or action</note> shall be completed so as not to sin anymore. And the likelihood of his former guardianship. Having a mind through the [one] before the healthy [one], may he fill him, I say, whoever commits adultery and does not repent...

<column-break/>

## Column 2

the righteous one, and if anyone should hear... when I had... what has happened he does not have. For indeed he receives in repentance the [forgiveness] of former stumblings. I was together with you and what I will give is nothing. That [is] a garden, he says to me. If indeed, he says, I am in repentance and I am with all who repent... it seems to me otherwise, what he says... this very thing to those who repent... to be the foundation of repentance. He says, understanding is great... for the sinner, having sinned... his [sin] comes... the evil thing [comes] before <term>the Lord</term> <note>original: KY, abbreviation for Kyriou</note> and it rises to his heart—the action which he did—and he repents and no longer works that which is evil. Instead, he does much good and works and will humble his own soul and torment it because he sinned. You see, then, that repentance is <margin>understanding</margin> <note>a marginal correction abbreviated as 'synes-', for synesis</note>. For this reason he says... do not be insincere... with you... first of all...

<summary>This page contains part of Mandate 4 from The Shepherd of Hermas, focusing on the definition of repentance as a form of "great understanding" (synesis). It discusses the psychological process of a sinner realizing their fault, feeling remorse, and turning toward good deeds to humble the soul.</summary>
<keywords>The Shepherd of Hermas, Mandate 4, repentance, understanding, synesis, sin, adultery, early Christian ethics, Codex Sinaiticus</keywords>

<meta>This page provides a scholarly index for the New Testament portion of the Codex Sinaiticus. While the previous page featured the primary text of "The Shepherd of Hermas," this index serves as a navigational tool for the entire facsimile volume, mapping the physical layout of the ancient manuscript to modern biblical chapters and verses. It covers the four Gospels, the Epistles of Paul, the Acts of the Apostles, the Catholic Epistles, Revelation, and the "Apocryphal" works included in this specific codex: the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas.</meta>
